72: Shopify APIs, libraries, and tools
73: Reference documentation for Shopify's APIs, libraries, and developer tools, plus the concepts that apply across all of them.
74: Authentication
75: How authentication works across Shopify's APIs, and which token and header each API uses.
76: Authentication
77: How authentication works across Shopify's APIs, and which token and header each API uses.
78: Authentication
79: How authentication works across Shopify's APIs, and which token and header each API uses.
80: Core concepts
81: Anchor to Know what applies to every APIKnow what applies to every API
82: Authentication, versioning, limits, and error handling work in similar ways across Shopify's APIs, though the details can differ from one API to the next. All Shopify APIs are subject to the Shopify API License and Terms of Use.
83: Authentication covers which token and header each API uses, and access scopes gate what that token can read and write. Some APIs also require Shopify's approval or a specific Shopify plan.
84: API versioning explains how Shopify releases a new version each quarter and supports each one for a year. You can find new features, breaking changes, and deprecations in the developer changelog.
85: Limits covers input array size, pagination depth, how rate limiting works, and where to find the rate limit figures for each API.
86: Response status and error codes are shared across APIs, and idempotent requests let you safely retry a request that might have failed.
87: Global IDs identify objects in the GraphQL APIs, cursor-based pagination walks long lists of them, and the search query syntax filters those lists.
88: Dev tools
89: Anchor to Set up your development environmentSet up your development environment
90: Shopify's tools generate a project, run it against a store while you work, deploy it, and give your AI agents the context to help.
91: Shopify CLI scaffolds apps, themes, and custom storefronts, runs them against a dev store while you work, and packages and releases your app versions.
92: The Dev Dashboard is where you create and manage apps, set up dev stores, and see how your app performs for merchants.
93: Shopify AI Toolkit connects AI coding tools, such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, to Shopify's developer docs, API schemas, and Shopify CLI, so they can help you build across the whole platform.
94: Shopify MCP lets merchants and partners set up and manage a store through the AI agent of their choice.
95: Dev stores are stores with test data that you build and test against.
96: React Router app package is Shopify's app package for React Router v7 and later.
97: Libraries and templates include official and community API libraries for Ruby, Node, PHP, Go, and .NET, plus app templates and sample apps.
98: App data and logic
99: Anchor to Read and write store dataRead and write store data
100: Your app reads and writes a store's data, runs its own logic on that data inside Shopify, and learns when something changes.
101: GraphQL Admin API reads and writes products, customers, orders, inventory, and the rest of the data behind the Shopify admin.
102: Events report object and field-level changes to GraphQL resources with highly configurable payloads, while classic webhooks notify your app when a store changes.
103: Shopify Functions run your own logic inside Shopify's backend for discounts, payments, and delivery.
104: ShopifyQL queries store data with SQL-like syntax and returns typed columns and rows.
105: Payments Apps API handles payment, capture, refund, and void sessions for payments partners.
106: Extensions and UI
107: Anchor to Extend every Shopify surfaceExtend every Shopify surface
108: Extensions render your app's interface inside Shopify's own surfaces, so it keeps working when Shopify changes the surface underneath it. Each surface has its own extension API.
109: App Home is the page merchants open your app on. Build it as an embedded page with App Bridge and Polaris, or as a UI extension with Preact.
110: Admin UI extensions add actions and blocks to pages in the Shopify admin.
111: Checkout UI extensions customize the buyer's path to purchase, and customer account UI extensions customize order status and profile pages.
112: POS UI extensions add your app to Shopify Point of Sale (POS), for staff selling in person.
113: Storefronts
114: Anchor to Build custom commerce experiencesBuild custom commerce experiences
115: Buyer-facing experiences run on Shopify's storefront APIs, frameworks, and template languages, from a Shopify theme to a storefront you host yourself.
116: Storefront API provides the commerce primitives for custom storefronts. Hydrogen is Shopify's toolkit for building headless storefronts in the framework of your choice, and Hydrogen React is the React library for legacy Hydrogen, versions 2026-04 and earlier.
117: Liquid is the template language for Shopify themes, and the Ajax API adds interactive elements, such as cart updates, without a full page reload.
118: Storefront Web Components bring Shopify-powered commerce to any website with HTML, and standard storefront events and actions give a storefront and the apps running on it a shared vocabulary.
119: Customer Account API provides access to customer identity and order history, and the Customer Privacy API records buyer consent.
120: App management
121: Anchor to Manage and monitor your appsManage and monitor your apps
122: The Dev Dashboard is where you configure a live app and watch how it's behaving. The APIs in this section cover the same ground programmatically.
123: Dev Dashboard creates and manages apps, stores, and catalogs, and its monitoring and logs chart webhooks, functions, and your own events.
124: Alerts in the Dev Dashboard flag apps that are making deprecated API calls, before a version removes them.
125: App Events API sends your app's own events to that monitoring, and reports usage for usage-based charges.
126: Partner API provides access to your Partner organization's business data, such as transactions and payouts.
127: Additional APIs
128: Anchor to Go deeper with specialized toolsGo deeper with specialized tools
129: Specialized tools cover specific surfaces and use cases: reaching shoppers in the Shop app, taking payments on sites that aren't on Shopify, measuring what buyers do, and reusing customer logins you already have.
130: Shop API connects your storefront to Shop, Shopify's consumer commerce surface, and Shop Minis are experiences that run inside the Shop app.
131: Shop Pay Wallet adds Shop Pay checkout to an ecommerce site that isn't on Shopify.
132: Web pixel app extensions collect behavioral data for marketing, optimization, and analytics.
133: Multipass manages customer authentication across multiple applications, so a customer who already logged in on your platform doesn't log in again.

123: Anchor to AuthenticationAuthentication
124: Every GraphQL Admin API request carries an access token in the X-Shopify-Access-Token header. For most apps you don't fetch or set that token yourself: the Shopify CLI template and Direct API access authenticate each request for you. To set up authentication for your app type, see About app authentication. For the token types and the grants that issue them, see access tokens.

520: Anchor to VersioningVersioning
521: The GraphQL Admin API is versioned. To keep your app stable, make sure that you specify a supported version in the URL.
522: Anchor to Rate limitsRate limits
523: The GraphQL Admin API is rate-limited using calculated query costs, measured in cost points. Each field returned by a query costs a set number of points. The total cost of a query is the maximum of possible fields selected, so more complex queries cost more to run.
524: Learn more about rate limits.

597: Anchor to Status and error codesStatus and error codes
598: All API queries return HTTP status codes that contain more information about the response.
599: Anchor to 200 OK200 OK
600: GraphQL HTTP status codes are different from REST API status codes. Most importantly, the GraphQL API can return a 200 OK response code in cases that would typically produce 4xx or 5xx errors in REST.
601: Anchor to Error handlingError handling
602: The response for the errors object contains additional detail to help you debug your operation.
603: The response for mutations contains additional detail to help debug your query. To access this, you must request userErrors.
604: Properties
605: errors•array
606: A list of all errors returned
607: Show error item properties
608: errors[n].message•string
609: Contains details about the error(s).
610: errors[n].extensions•object
611: Provides more information about the error(s) including properties and metadata.
612: Show extensions properties
613: errors[n].extensions.code•string
614: Shows error codes common to Shopify. Additional error codes may also be shown.
615: Show common error codes
616: THROTTLED
617: The client has exceeded the rate limit. Similar to 429 Too Many Requests.
618: ACCESS_DENIED
619: The client doesn’t have correct authentication credentials. Similar to 401 Unauthorized.
620: SHOP_INACTIVE
621: The shop is not active. This can happen when stores repeatedly exceed API rate limits or due to fraud risk.
622: INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR
623: Shopify experienced an internal error while processing the request. This error is returned instead of 500 Internal Server Error in most circumstances.
624: Anchor to 4xx and 5xx status codes4xx and 5xx status codes
625: The 4xx and 5xx errors occur infrequently. They are often related to network communications, your account, or an issue with Shopify’s services.
626: Many errors that would typically return a 4xx or 5xx status code, return an HTTP 200 errors response instead. Refer to the 200 OK section above for details.

61: This tutorial shows how to use the client credentials grant to get access tokens for a server-side app acting on stores in your own Shopify organization. Of the three grants, it takes the least setup: your app exchanges its own client ID and secret for a token, with no redirect flow to implement.
62: With a client credentials grant, you won't see a token in the Shopify admin. Instead, you request tokens programmatically when you need them.
63: Info
64: If you're building apps for other merchants, use Shopify CLI, which handles authentication automatically. To authenticate with a key pair instead of your client secret, or to get tokens for any store that has installed an app with public distribution, see Get application-only access tokens for installed stores. To learn how authentication works for other common approaches, see About app authentication.

269: Anchor to Exchange credentials for a tokenExchange credentials for a token
270: The code reads your credentials from the environment and exchanges them for an access token. Tokens expire after 24 hours, so the example caches the token and refreshes it before expiry rather than requesting a new one per call.
271: Caution
272: Don't send a scope parameter. Shopify ignores it: the token always carries all the access scopes that the store granted to your app installation, which might be broader than the scopes you send. Read the scope field in the response to see what the token carries.
273: Caution:
274: Don't send a scope parameter. Shopify ignores it: the token always carries all the access scopes that the store granted to your app installation, which might be broader than the scopes you send. Read the scope field in the response to see what the token carries.
275: Token response format
276: Copy
277: 1
278: 2
279: 3
280: 4
281: 5
282: {
283: "access_token": "f85632530bf277ec9ac6f649fc327f17",
284: "scope": "read_products",
285: "expires_in": 86399
286: }
287: access_token: The token to include in API requests. Store this securely.
288: scope: The access scopes that the store granted to your app installation, which is what the token carries. It isn't a readback of a scope parameter you send, and it isn't every scope your app declares on its version: an optional scope that the store declined or revoked doesn't appear. If a scope you need is missing, release a new version with it and approve the change on the store.
289: expires_in: Seconds until expiration. Always 86399 (24 hours).
290: Troubleshooting
291: Anchor to shop_not_permitted errorshop_not_permitted error
292: Problem: You receive the error Oauth error shop_not_permitted: Client credentials cannot be performed on this shop.
293: Solution: The client credentials grant only works when the app and the store belong to the same Shopify organization. "Same organization" means both appear under the same org in the Dev Dashboard. Owning a store or having it installed doesn't automatically place it in your org.
294: To verify:
295: Open the Dev Dashboard and click Apps. Confirm your app is listed.
296: Click Dev stores in the sidebar and confirm your target store appears in the list. If the store isn't listed, it's not in this organization.
297: Check that your SHOPIFY_SHOP value matches the store's *.myshopify.com subdomain exactly (without .myshopify.com).
298: Common causes:
299: Dev store created outside the Dev Dashboard: If you created a dev store from the Shopify admin rather than from the Dev Dashboard, it won't be in your org. Create a new dev store from the Dev stores page in the Dev Dashboard instead.
300: Multiple organizations: If you have access to more than one organization, the app and store might be in different ones. Check the organization ID in the URL (dev.shopify.com/dashboard/<org-id>) and verify both the app and store are under the same one.
301: Acting on another organization's stores: The client credentials grant can't reach a store outside your organization, including a client's store, unless your app has public distribution and authenticates with a client assertion. Distribute your app to that store with custom distribution so that a merchant installs it, then use token exchange if your app runs inside the Shopify admin, or the authorization code grant if it runs outside. Shopify CLI handles OAuth for you. If your app has public distribution and the store has already installed it, then it can also get application-only access tokens with a client assertion.
302: Anchor to External tool asks you to "copy a token"External tool asks you to "copy a token"
303: Problem: Some external tools ask you to copy a token or provide a "Shopify API key." These tools expect the older authentication flow.
304: Solution: Contact the tool vendor about updating their integration to use OAuth.
305: Anchor to "Invalid API key or access token" error"Invalid API key or access token" error
306: Problem: You're sending your client_id or client_secret directly to the GraphQL Admin API.
307: Solution: First exchange your credentials for an access_token using the token endpoint, then use that token in your API requests.

68: Dev stores are testing environments that you own and control. They let you build and test your apps in a realistic Shopify environment without affecting any live store. You can connect directly to a dev store from Shopify CLI using the shopify app dev command, which previews your changes without deploying a new version to production.
69: Anchor to RequirementsRequirements
70: Before you begin, make sure you have the following accounts and permissions:
71: A Shopify Partner account or a merchant store with developer permissions.
72: The required permissions to create dev stores in your organization.
73: Anchor to Create a dev storeCreate a dev store
74: If your organization has a primary business entity, which you set in Organization settings > Organization > Organization business details, then new dev stores are created in its country and use that entity. If it doesn't have one yet, then new dev stores get their own business entity with the business type Unspecified. If you switch your organization's primary business entity, then dev stores that you create afterward use the new one. Existing dev stores keep their current entity.
75: You can create a dev store with Shopify CLI, or start from the Dev Dashboard.
76: Anchor to Use Shopify CLIUse Shopify CLI
77: The Shopify CLI store create dev command creates new dev stores in your organization.
78: The command will prompt you for required values, or you can configure the store via flags:
79: FlagDescription
80: --nameThe name for the store. This name is used to identify the store and create the store's myshopify.com URL. You can't change the myshopify.com URL after the store is created.
81: --planThe Shopify plan to use: basic, grow, advanced, or plus.
82: --demo-dataPopulates the store with demo data so you're not testing against an empty store.
83: --feature-previewThe handle of a feature preview to enable on the store.
84: --countryThe store's two-letter ISO country code, such as US, CA, or GB.
85: If you pass --country with a country other than your primary business entity's, then the store doesn't use your primary business entity. It gets its own business entity with the business type Unspecified.
86: For example, the following command creates a Plus plan store in Canada, populated with demo data:
87: Terminal
88: Copy
89: 1
90: shopify store create dev --name "Checkout testing" --plan plus --demo-data --country CA
91: Anchor to Use the Dev DashboardUse the Dev Dashboard
92: Create store opens the store setup flow in Shopify admin. When setup completes, the store appears in the Dev Dashboard's Stores list.
93: Log in to the Dev Dashboard.
94: Select Stores from the left sidebar.
95: Select Create store, then select Dev as the store type.
96: Enter a name for your dev store. This name is used to identify the store in the Dev Dashboard and sets the store's myshopify.com URL.
97: Caution
98: You can't change a dev store's myshopify.com URL after the store is created.
99: Caution:
100: You can't change a dev store's myshopify.com URL after the store is created.
101: Select a plan for your dev store:
102: Basic: Includes core Shopify features for small businesses.
103: Grow: Includes additional reporting and staff accounts for growing businesses.
104: Advanced: Includes advanced reporting, lower transaction fees, and third-party calculated shipping rates.
105: Plus: Includes enterprise-level features like Shopify Flow, LaunchPad, and dedicated support.
106: Optional: Select Test a feature preview to test capabilities that aren't available to all stores yet.
107: Select Create store to finish setup.
108: Log in to your dev store.
109: Anchor to Store accessStore access
110: When you create a dev store, you're automatically designated as the store's owner. Shopify CLI and Dev Dashboard display dev stores that you have access to.
111: Additional users must be added to the store as staff members.
112: Info
113: To install third-party apps on a dev store, you or the owner of your organization need to verify your identity. Apps that your organization owns are exempt from this requirement.
114: Info:
115: To install third-party apps on a dev store, you or the owner of your organization need to verify your identity. Apps that your organization owns are exempt from this requirement.
116: When a feature preview is enabled on a dev store, you don't have access to domains.
117: Anchor to Clean up dev storesClean up dev stores
118: Organizations are limited to 250 dev stores. You can use Shopify CLI to list dev stores in your organization, and delete stores you no longer need.
119: List the stores in your organization using the shopify store list command:
120: Terminal
121: Copy
122: 1
123: shopify store list
124: To delete a store, pass its myshopify.com domain to the shopify store delete command:
125: Terminal
126: Copy
127: 1
128: shopify store delete --store my-dev-store.myshopify.com
129: Anchor to Example: Delete stores older than two yearsExample: Delete stores older than two years
130: Use the --json flag with shopify store list to filter and script the command output. Each entry includes store, type, and createdAt, so the following deletes every dev store created more than two years ago:
131: Terminal
132: Copy
133: 1
134: 2
135: 3
136: 4
137: 5
138: shopify store list --type dev --json \
139: | jq -r '.stores[]
140: | select((.createdAt | fromdateiso8601) < (now - 2*365*86400))
141: | .store' \
142: | xargs -I{} shopify store delete --store {} --force
143: In this example:
144: --type dev matters on a large organization. The command returns at most 250 stores, newest first, so the old dev stores you're trying to delete are the ones that fall off the end. Filtering by type on the server keeps them in range.
145: createdAt is when the store was created, not when it was last opened.
146: Caution
147: Deleting a dev store is permanent. The store and its data are purged, and can't be restored.
148: Caution:
149: Deleting a dev store is permanent. The store and its data are purged, and can't be restored.
150: Anchor to LimitationsLimitations
151: Dev stores are for development and testing only. They can't be used in production or process real transactions. The following limitations and testing requirements apply:
152: For apps that use App Pricing, you can select any available plan for an app that belongs to your Partner organization at no charge. For apps from another Partner organization, you can select free plans or any plan the Partner has marked as free to test.
153: For an app that uses manual pricing, use a Billing API test charge to test your own app. To make the app available on other Partners' dev stores, set up free testing.
154: You can test orders using Shopify's Test payment gateway or by activating test mode for your payment provider. Real transactions through active payment providers, Store Credit, and Gift Cards aren't supported.
155: Dev stores are always password protected. You can't remove the password page or replace it with a custom one. Your theme's customizable password page is a separate page: it doesn't control access to a dev store, but you can edit and preview it.
156: You can't change a dev store's myshopify.com URL after the store is created. To use a different URL, create a new dev store.
157: Dev stores can't be converted to production stores.
158: Dev stores can't be transferred to a client. If you're building a store for a merchant, use a client transfer store instead.

38: Anchor to From product discovery to purchaseFrom product discovery to purchase
39: With Shop MCP, bring the shopping journey into your agent or app, from product discovery and carts to checkout and order history. You don't need an API key or a custom UCP profile.
40: Find the right products: Search the catalog and view product details without buyer sign-in. With Shop sign-in, use the buyer's saved preferences to help find products that fit.
41: Build a cart: Add and update products as buyers decide what to buy. Create a checkout when they're ready, with one checkout per merchant.
42: Complete the purchase: Without Shop sign-in, buyers review and pay on the merchant's checkout page. With Shop sign-in, your agent completes checkout after the buyer confirms the total and selects a payment method.
43: Check order history: After a buyer signs in with Shop, search their Shop-tracked orders to answer questions in the same conversation.
44: Learn what your agent can do with Shop MCP, or compare integration options.
45: Anchor to Choose your pathChoose your path
46: Most agents and apps should start with Shop MCP, Shopify's hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server:
47: Shop MCP: Use to search products, build carts, check out, accept Shop Pay, personalize results, view order history, or earn commission on sales. Shop MCP can be used whether buyers sign in with Shop, connect your platform's accounts to their Shop accounts, or shop without sign-in.
48: Depending on your platform's needs, other options for agents include:
49: UCP directly: The Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) is an open standard for agents to shop on behalf of buyers. Use UCP directly to identify buyers only through your platform's accounts, without asking them to connect a Shop account.
50: Global Catalog or Storefront Catalog: Global Catalog and Storefront Catalog are MCP servers for product discovery across Shopify merchants and within a single merchant's storefront, respectively. Use these catalog tools to replace Shopify's product ranking with your own, using Shopify product data. Sorting or filtering Shop MCP results doesn't require this.
51: Catalog API: The Catalog API provides direct access to Shopify's Global Catalog for product search. Use it to search products when you don't need accounts, carts, or checkout.
52: When you use UCP directly, your platform manages buyer identity, consent, any custom product ranking, and order reconciliation. Completing checkout within your agent requires Shopify's permission. Without that permission, buyers complete their purchase on the merchant's checkout page.
53: Shop MCP handles these parts of the integration for you. It's the recommended starting point for most agents and apps. Learn how to connect your agent to Shop MCP.

367: What is Shopify and how does it work?
368: Shopify is an all-in-one commerce platform that lets you create an online store, accept payments, and sell in person, on social channels, and in AI chats—all from one dashboard. Chat your store into existence or start from a theme, manage products and inventory, process orders and shipping, and let Sidekick, your very own commerce AI, take on marketing, analytics, and everyday admin—from web or mobile, no coding required.
369: What AI comes with Shopify?
370: Every plan includes Sidekick, your very own commerce AI, plus generous AI usage to build and run your store. Design your store by chatting with AI, connect the AI tools you already use, or build with Shopify CLI. And your products can show up in AI chats, ready for shoppers to buy.
371: How much does Shopify cost?
372: Shopify starts with a free 3-day trial—no credit card required. After your trial, most plans start at just ₹20 per month for the first 3 months, then switch to standard monthly pricing.
373: Additionally, you can choose to add POS Pro to your subscription for more advanced point of sale features like staff roles and permissions, exchanges, and flexible customer pickup and delivery options.
374: Can I cancel or change my subscription anytime?
375: Yes. If you ever decide that Shopify isn't the best commerce platform for your business, simply cancel your account.
376: If you choose a 1- or 3-year Plus subscription, you can cancel when your term commitment expires.
377: Are there any additional fees?
378: There are no setup fees on any of our plans.
379: Third-party transaction fees may apply when you use a third-party payment provider (instead of Shopify Payments). The rate depends on your plan.
380: Shopify charges a small fee to allow you to accept major credit cards, such as Visa and Mastercard, as payment in your store. These fees vary depending on the plan that you choose.
381: In what countries can I use Shopify?
382: Shopify is available in nearly every country in the world. Some features vary by country—for example, Shopify Payments is available only in certain countries—so pricing and payment options can differ depending on where your business is based.
383: Is Shopify PCI Compliant or PCI Certified?
384: Yes. Shopify is certified Level 1 PCI DSS compliant, and stores powered by Shopify are PCI compliant by default, which helps keep payment information secure.
385: Can I use my own domain name with Shopify?
386: Yes. You can use a domain you already own, or buy a new one. Every Shopify store also comes with a free myshopify.com address, and Shopify helps keep your site secure automatically.
387: If you already have a domain, you can keep it where you bought it and simply connect it to Shopify—or move it to Shopify so everything is managed in one place.
388: Do I get web hosting with Shopify?
389: Yes. Shopify includes secure commerce hosting with your Shopify plan, so you don't need to buy separate hosting. Shopify also includes unlimited bandwidth (no bandwidth fees) and provides a free TLS/SSL certificate for domains you add to Shopify.
390: Additionally, you can use the Buy Button sales channel to embed buy buttons on an external website or blog, and let customers check out using Shopify Checkout.

18: WooCommerce REST API
19: WooCommerce (WC) 2.6+ is fully integrated with the WordPress REST API. This allows WC data to be created, read, updated, and deleted using requests in JSON format and using WordPress REST API Authentication methods and standard HTTP verbs which are understood by most HTTP clients.
20: The current WP REST API integration version is v3 which takes a first-order position in endpoints.
21: When WooPayments is active, it adds payment-specific endpoints under /wp-json/wc/v3/payments/. See the WooPayments REST API reference for transactions, authorizations, and payouts. Some monetary fields in these endpoints use integer minor units, unlike WooCommerce core's decimal-string values.
22: Requirements​
23: To use the REST API you must be using:
24: WooCommerce 3.5+
25: WordPress 4.4+
26: Pretty permalinks in Settings > Permalinks (default permalinks will not work)
27: You may access the API over either HTTP or HTTPS, but HTTPS is recommended where possible.
28: note
29: You are not required to install the WP REST API (WP API) plugin.
30: If you use ModSecurity and see 501 Method Not Implemented errors, see this issue for details.
31: Libraries and tools​
32: Official libraries​
33: JavaScript Library
34: PHP Library
35: Python Library
36: Ruby Library
37: JavaScript
38: PHP
39: Python
40: Ruby

42: // npm install --save @woocommerce/woocommerce-rest-api

44: const WooCommerceRestApi = require("@woocommerce/woocommerce-rest-api").default;

46: const WooCommerce = new WooCommerceRestApi({

92: Third party libraries​
93: Java Library
94: .NET Library
95: Android Library
96: note
97: We don't offer support for third party libraries. If you have questions about how to use any of these libraries, contact the respective authors.
98: Tools​
99: Insomnia - Cross-platform GraphQL and REST client, available for Mac, Windows, and Linux.
100: Postman - Cross-platform REST client, available for Mac, Windows, and Linux.
101: RequestBin - Allows you test webhooks.
102: Hookbin - Another tool to test webhooks.
103: Generate keys​
104: To start using REST API, you first need to generate API keys.
105: Go to WooCommerce > Settings > Advanced
106: Go to the REST API tab and click Add key
107: Give the key a description for your own reference, choose a user with access to orders etc, and give the key read/write permissions
108: Click Generate API key
109: Your keys will be shown - do not close this tab yet, the secret will be hidden if you try to view the key again
110: Make a basic request​
111: The request URL we'll test is wp-json/wc/v3/orders. On localhost the full URL may look something like this: https://localhost:8888/wp-json/wc/v3/orders. Modify this to use your own site URL.
112: In Postman, you need to set the fields for request type, request URL, and the settings on the authorization tab. For Authorization, choose basic auth and enter your consumer key and consumer secret keys from WooCommerce into the username and password fields.
113: Once done, hit send and you'll see the JSON response from the API if all worked well:
114: Insomnia is almost identical to Postman; fill in the same fields and again use basic auth:
115: Request/Response format​
116: The default response format is JSON. Requests with a message-body use plain JSON to set or update resource attributes. Successful requests will return a 200 OK HTTP status.
117: Some general information about responses:
118: Dates are returned in ISO8601 format: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS
119: Resource IDs are returned as integers
120: Any decimal monetary amount, such as prices or totals, will be returned as strings with two decimal places
121: Other amounts, such as item counts, are returned as integers
122: Blank fields are generally included as null or empty string instead of being omitted
123: JSONP support​
124: The WP REST API supports JSONP by default. JSONP responses use the application/javascript content-type. You can specify the callback using the ?_jsonp parameter for GET requests to have the response wrapped in a JSON function:
125: GET /wp-json/wc/v3?_jsonp=callback
126: Parameters​
127: Almost all endpoints accept optional parameters which can be passed as a HTTP query string parameter, e.g. GET /orders?status=completed. All parameters are documented along each endpoint.
128: Pagination​
129: Requests that return multiple items will be paginated to 10 items by default. This default can be changed by the site administrator by changing the posts_per_page option. Alternatively the items per page can be specified with the ?per_page parameter:
130: GET /orders?per_page=15
131: You can specify further pages with the ?page parameter:
132: GET /orders?page=2
133: You may also specify the offset from the first resource using the ?offset parameter:
134: GET /orders?offset=5
135: Page number is 1-based and omitting the ?page parameter will return the first page.
136: The total number of resources and pages are always included in the X-WP-Total and X-WP-TotalPages HTTP headers.
137: Link header​
138: Pagination info is included in the Link Header. It's recommended that you follow these values instead of building your own URLs where possible.
139: Link: <https://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products?page=2>; rel="next",
140: <https://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products?page=3>; rel="last"
141: ValueDescription
142: nextShows the URL of the immediate next page of results.
143: lastShows the URL of the last page of results.
144: firstShows the URL of the first page of results.
145: prevShows the URL of the immediate previous page of results.
146: Errors​
147: Occasionally you might encounter errors when accessing the REST API. There are four possible types:
148: Error CodeError Type
149: 400 Bad RequestInvalid request, e.g. using an unsupported HTTP method
150: 401 UnauthorizedAuthentication or permission error, e.g. incorrect API keys
151: 404 Not FoundRequests to resources that don't exist or are missing
152: 500 Internal Server ErrorServer error
153: Errors return both an appropriate HTTP status code and response object which contains a code, message and data attribute:
154: {
155: "code": "woocommerce_rest_term_invalid",
156: "message": "Resource doesn't exist.",
157: "data": {
158: "status": 404
159: }
160: }
161: Common connection issues​
162: Connection issues with localhost and self-signed SSL certificates​
163: If you're having problems connecting to the REST API on your localhost and seeing SSL errors, you need to disable SSL verification.
164: In Postman you can find this in the settings:
165: Insomnia also has this setting in the preferences area:
166: 401 Unauthorized​
167: Your API keys or signature is wrong. Ensure that:
168: The user you generated API keys for actually has access to those resources
169: The username when authenticating is your consumer key
170: The password when authenticating is your consumer secret
171: Make a new set of keys to be sure
172: If your server utilizes FastCGI, check that your authorization headers are properly read.
173: Consumer key is missing​
174: Occasionally servers may not parse the Authorization header correctly (if you see a "Consumer key is missing" error when authenticating over SSL, you have a server issue).
175: In this case, you may provide the consumer key/secret as query string parameters instead:
176: https://local.wordpress.dev/wp-json/wc/v2/orders?consumer_key=XXXX&consumer_secret=XXXX
177: Server does not support POST/DELETE/PUT​
178: Ideally, your server should be configured to accept these types of API request, but if not you can use the _method property.
179: API version history​
180: API VersionWC VersionWP Version
181: v33.5.x or later4.4 or later
182: v23.0.x or later4.4 or later
183: v12.6.x or later4.4 or later
184: Learn more​
185: Learn more about the REST API checking the official WordPress REST API documentation.

267: To use the latest version of the REST API you must be using:
268: WooCommerce 3.5+.
269: WordPress 4.4+.
270: Pretty permalinks in Settings > Permalinks so that the custom endpoints are supported. Default permalinks will not work.
271: You may access the API over either HTTP or HTTPS, but HTTPS is recommended where possible.
272: If you use ModSecurity and see 501 Method Not Implemented errors, see this issue for details.
273: Please note that you are not required to install the WP REST API (WP API) plugin.
274: Request/Response Format
275: The default response format is JSON. Requests with a message-body use plain JSON to set or update resource attributes. Successful requests will return a 200 OK HTTP status.
276: Some general information about responses:
277: Dates are returned in ISO8601 format: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS
278: Resource IDs are returned as integers.
279: Any decimal monetary amount, such as prices or totals, will be returned as strings with two decimal places.
280: Other amounts, such as item counts, are returned as integers.
281: Blank fields are generally included as null or emtpy string instead of being omitted.
282: JSONP Support
283: The WP REST API supports JSONP by default. JSONP responses use the application/javascript content-type. You can specify the callback using the ?_jsonp parameter for GET requests to have the response wrapped in a JSON function:
284: GET
285: /wp-json/wc/v3?_jsonp=callback
286: curl https://example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products/tags/34?_jsonp=tagDetails \
287: -u consumer_key:consumer_secret
288: WooCommerce.get("products/tags/34?_jsonp=tagDetails")
289: .then((response) => {
290: console.log(response.data);
291: })
292: .catch((error) => {
293: console.log(error.response.data);
294: });
295: <?php print_r($woocommerce->get('products/tags/34', ['_jsonp' => 'tagDetails'])); ?>
296: print(wcapi.get("products/tags/34?_jsonp=tagDetails").json())
297: woocommerce.get("products/tags/34", _jsonp: "tagDetails").parsed_response
298: Response:
299: /**/tagDetails({"id":34,"name":"Leather Shoes","slug":"leather-shoes","description":"","count":0,"_links":{"self":[{"href":"https://example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products/tags/34"}],"collection":[{"href":"https://example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products/tags"}]}})%
300: Errors
301: Occasionally you might encounter errors when accessing the REST API. There are four possible types:
302: Error Code
303: Error Type
304: 400 Bad Request
305: Invalid request, e.g. using an unsupported HTTP method
306: 401 Unauthorized
307: Authentication or permission error, e.g. incorrect API keys
308: 404 Not Found
309: Requests to resources that don't exist or are missing
310: 500 Internal Server Error
311: Server error
312: WP REST API error example:
313: {
314: "code": "rest_no_route",
315: "message": "No route was found matching the URL and request method",
316: "data": {
317: "status": 404
318: }
319: }
320: WooCommerce REST API error example:
321: {
322: "code": "woocommerce_rest_term_invalid",
323: "message": "Resource doesn't exist.",
324: "data": {
325: "status": 404
326: }
327: }
328: Errors return both an appropriate HTTP status code and response object which contains a code, message and data attribute.
329: Parameters
330: Almost all endpoints accept optional parameters which can be passed as a HTTP query string parameter, e.g. GET /orders?status=completed. All parameters are documented along each endpoint.
331: Pagination
332: Requests that return multiple items will be paginated to 10 items by default. This default can be changed by the site administrator by changing the posts_per_page option. Alternatively the items per page can be specified with the ?per_page parameter:
333: GET /orders?per_page=15
334: You can specify further pages with the ?page parameter:
335: GET /orders?page=2
336: You may also specify the offset from the first resource using the ?offset parameter:
337: GET /orders?offset=5
338: Page number is 1-based and omitting the ?page parameter will return the first page.
339: The total number of resources and pages are always included in the X-WP-Total and X-WP-TotalPages HTTP headers.
340: Link Header
341: Pagination info is included in the Link Header. It's recommended that you follow these values instead of building your own URLs where possible.
342: Link: <https://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products?page=2>; rel="next",
343: <https://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products?page=3>; rel="last"`
344: The possible rel values are:
345: Value
346: Description
347: next
348: Shows the URL of the immediate next page of results.
349: last
350: Shows the URL of the last page of results.
351: first
352: Shows the URL of the first page of results.
353: prev
354: Shows the URL of the immediate previous page of results.

426: Authentication
427: WooCommerce includes two ways to authenticate with the WP REST API. It is also possible to authenticate using any WP REST API authentication plugin or method.
428: REST API keys
429: Pre-generated keys can be used to authenticate use of the REST API endpoints. New keys can be generated either through the WordPress admin interface or they can be auto-generated through an endpoint.
430: Generating API keys in the WordPress admin interface
431: To create or manage keys for a specific WordPress user, go to WooCommerce > Settings > Advanced > REST API.
432: Note: Keys/Apps was found at WooCommerce > Settings > API > Key/Apps prior to WooCommerce 3.4.
433: Click the "Add Key" button. In the next screen, add a description and select the WordPress user you would like to generate the key for. Use of the REST API with the generated keys will conform to that user's WordPress roles and capabilities.
434: Choose the level of access for this REST API key, which can be Read access, Write access or Read/Write access. Then click the "Generate API Key" button and WooCommerce will generate REST API keys for the selected user.
435: Now that keys have been generated, you should see two new keys, a QRCode, and a Revoke API Key button. These two keys are your Consumer Key and Consumer Secret.
436: If the WordPress user associated with an API key is deleted, the API key will cease to function. API keys are not transferred to other users.
437: Auto generating API keys using our Application Authentication Endpoint
438: This endpoint can be used by any APP to allow users to generate API keys for your APP. This makes integration with WooCommerce API easier because the user only needs to grant access to your APP via a URL. After being redirected back to your APP, the API keys will be sent back in a separate POST request.

440: This endpoint works exclusively for users to generate API keys and facilitate integration between the WooCommerce REST API and an application. In no way is this endpoint intended to be used as login method for customers.

624: Authentication over HTTP
625: You must use OAuth 1.0a "one-legged" authentication to ensure REST API credentials cannot be intercepted by an attacker. Typically you will use any standard OAuth 1.0a library in the language of your choice to handle the authentication, or generate the necessary parameters by following the following instructions.
626: Creating a signature
627: Collect the request method and URL
628: First you need to determine the HTTP method you will be using for the request, and the URL of the request.
629: The HTTP method will be GET in our case.
630: The Request URL will be the endpoint you are posting to, e.g. http://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/orders.
631: Collect parameters
632: Collect and normalize your parameters. This includes all oauth_* parameters except for the oauth_signature itself.
633: These values need to be encoded into a single string which will be used later on. The process to build the string is very specific:
634: Percent encode every key and value that will be signed.
635: Sort the list of parameters alphabetically by encoded key.
636: For each key/value pair:
637: Append the encoded key to the output string.
638: Append the = character to the output string.
639: Append the encoded value to the output string.
640: If there are more key/value pairs remaining, append a & character to the output string.
641: When percent encoding in PHP for example, you would use rawurlencode().
642: When sorting parameters in PHP for example, you would use uksort( $params, 'strcmp' ).
643: Parameters example:
644: oauth_consumer_key=abc123&oauth_signature_method=HMAC-SHA1
645: Create the signature base string
646: The above values collected so far must be joined to make a single string, from which the signature will be generated. This is called the signature base string in the OAuth specification.
647: To encode the HTTP method, request URL, and parameter string into a single string:
648: Set the output string equal to the uppercase HTTP Method.
649: Append the & character to the output string.
650: Percent encode the URL and append it to the output string.
651: Append the & character to the output string.
652: Percent encode the parameter string and append it to the output string.
653: Example signature base string:
654: GET&http%3A%2F%2Fwww.example.com%2Fwp-json%2Fwc%2Fv3%2Forders&oauth_consumer_key%3Dabc123%26oauth_signature_method%3DHMAC-SHA1
655: Generate the signature
656: Generate the signature using the signature base string and your consumer secret key with a & character with the HMAC-SHA1 hashing algorithm.
657: In PHP you can use the hash_hmac function.
658: HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-SHA256 are the only accepted hash algorithms.
659: If you are having trouble generating a correct signature, you'll want to review the string you are signing for encoding errors. The authentication source can also be helpful in understanding how to properly generate the signature.
660: OAuth tips
661: The OAuth parameters may be added as query string parameters or included in the Authorization header.
662: Note there is no reliable cross-platform way to get the raw request headers in WordPress, so query string should be more reliable in some cases.
663: The required parameters are: oauth_consumer_key, oauth_timestamp, oauth_nonce, oauth_signature, and oauth_signature_method. oauth_version is not required and should be omitted.
664: The OAuth nonce can be any randomly generated 32 character (recommended) string that is unique to the consumer key.
665: The OAuth timestamp should be the unix timestamp at the time of the request. The REST API will deny any requests that include a timestamp outside of a 15 minute window to prevent replay attacks.
666: You must use the store URL provided by the index when forming the base string used for the signature, as this is what the server will use. (e.g. if the store URL includes a www sub-domain, you should use it for requests)
667: Note that the request body is not signed as per the OAuth spec.
668: If including parameters in your request, it saves a lot of trouble if you can order your items alphabetically.
669: Authorization header is supported starting WooCommerce 3.0.

16620: Order actions
16621: The order actions API allows you to perform specific actions with existing orders like you can from the Edit Order screen in the web app.
16622: Note: currently only some actions are available, other actions will be introduced at a later time.
16623: Send order details to customer
16624: This endpoint allows you to trigger an email to the customer with the details of their order. In case the order doesn't yet have a billing email set, you can specify an email recipient. However, if the order does have an existing billing email, this will return an error, unless you also specify that the existing email should be overwritten by using the force_email_update parameter.
16625: HTTP request
16626: POST
16627: /wp-json/wc/v3/orders/<id>/actions/send_order_details
16628: curl -X POST https://example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/orders/723/actions/send_order_details \
16629: -u consumer_key:consumer_secret \
16630: -d '{
16631: "email": "somebody@example.com",
16632: "force_email_update": true
16633: }'
16634: const data = {
16635: email: "somebody@example.com",
16636: force_email_update: true
16637: };
16638: WooCommerce.post("orders/723/actions/send_order_details", data)
16639: .then((response) => {
16640: console.log(response.data);
16641: })
16642: .catch((error) => {
16643: console.log(error.response.data);
16644: });
16645: <?php
16646: $data = [
16647: 'email' => 'somebody@example.com',
16648: 'force_email_update' => true,
16649: ];
16650: print_r($woocommerce->post('orders/723/actions/send_order_details', $data));
16651: ?>
16652: data = {
16653: "email": "somebody@example.com",
16654: "force_email_update": true
16655: }
16656: print(wcapi.post("orders/723/actions/send_order_details", data).json())
16657: data = {
16658: "email": "somebody@example.com",
16659: "force_email_update": true
16660: }
16661: woocommerce.post("orders/723/actions/send_order_details", data).parsed_response

16663: {
16664: "message": "Billing email updated to somebody@example.com. Order details sent to somebody@example.com, via REST API."
16665: }
16666: {
16667: "code": "woocommerce_rest_missing_email",
16668: "message": "Order does not have an email address.",
16669: "data": {
16670: "status": 400
16671: }
16672: }
16673: Send order notification email to customer
16674: This endpoint allows you to trigger an email to a customer about the status of their order. This is similar to the send_order_details endpoint, but allows you to specify which email template to send, based on which email templates are relevant to the order. For example, an order that is on hold has the customer_on_hold_order template available. A completed order that also has a partial refund has both the customer_completed_order and customer_refunded_order templates available. Specifying the customer_invoice template is the same as using the send_order_details endpoint.
16675: HTTP request
16676: POST
16677: /wp-json/wc/v3/orders/<id>/actions/send_email
16678: curl -X POST https://example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/orders/723/actions/send_email \
16679: -u consumer_key:consumer_secret \
16680: -d '{
16681: "template_id": "customer_completed_order",
16682: "email": "somebody@example.com",
16683: "force_email_update": true
16684: }'
16685: const data = {
16686: template_id: "customer_completed_order",
16687: email: "somebody@example.com",
16688: force_email_update: true
16689: };
16690: WooCommerce.post("orders/723/actions/send_email", data)
16691: .then((response) => {
16692: console.log(response.data);
16693: })
16694: .catch((error) => {
16695: console.log(error.response.data);
16696: });
16697: <?php
16698: $data = [
16699: 'template_id' => 'customer_completed_order',
16700: 'email' => 'somebody@example.com',
16701: 'force_email_update' => true,
16702: ];
16703: print_r($woocommerce->post('orders/723/actions/send_email', $data));
16704: ?>
16705: data = {
16706: "template_id": "customer_completed_order",
16707: "email": "somebody@example.com",
16708: "force_email_update": true
16709: }
16710: print(wcapi.post("orders/723/actions/send_email", data).json())
16711: data = {
16712: "template_id": "customer_completed_order",

16714: "force_email_update": true
16715: }

22301: Product attributes
22302: The product attributes API allows you to create, view, update, and delete individual, or a batch, of product attributes.
22303: Product attribute properties
22304: Attribute
22305: Type
22306: Description
22307: id
22308: integer
22309: Unique identifier for the resource. read-only
22310: name
22311: string
22312: Attribute name. mandatory
22313: slug
22314: string
22315: An alphanumeric identifier for the resource unique to its type.
22316: type
22317: string
22318: Type of attribute. By default only select is supported.
22319: order_by
22320: string
22321: Default sort order. Options: menu_order, name, name_num and id. Default is menu_order.
22322: has_archives
22323: boolean
22324: Enable/Disable attribute archives. Default is false.
22325: Create a product attribute
22326: This API helps you to create a new product attribute.
22327: HTTP request
22328: POST
22329: /wp-json/wc/v3/products/attributes

22331: -u consumer_key:consumer_secret \
22332: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
22333: -d '{
22334: "name": "Color",
22335: "slug": "pa_color",
22336: "type": "select",
22337: "order_by": "menu_order",
22338: "has_archives": true
22339: }'

31070: Webhooks
31071: The webhooks API allows you to create, view, update, and delete individual, or a batch, of webhooks.
31072: Webhooks can be managed via the WooCommerce settings screen or by using the REST API endpoints. The WC_Webhook class manages all data storage and retrieval of the webhook custom post type, as well as enqueuing webhook actions and processing/delivering/logging webhooks. On woocommerce_init, active webhooks are loaded.
31073: Each webhook has:
31074: status: active (delivers payload), paused (delivery paused by admin), disabled (delivery paused by failure).
31075: topic: determines which resource events the webhook is triggered for.
31076: delivery URL: URL where the payload is delivered, must be HTTP or HTTPS.
31077: secret: an optional secret key that is used to generate a HMAC-SHA256 hash of the request body so the receiver can verify authenticity of the webhook.
31078: hooks: an array of hook names that are added and bound to the webhook for processing.
31079: Topics
31080: The topic is a combination resource (e.g. order) and event (e.g. created) and maps to one or more hook names (e.g. woocommerce_checkout_order_processed). Webhooks can be created using the topic name and the appropriate hooks are automatically added.
31081: Core topics are:
31082: Coupons: coupon.created, coupon.updated and coupon.deleted.
31083: Customers: customer.created, customer.updated and customer.deleted.
31084: Orders: order.created, order.updated and order.deleted.
31085: Products: product.created, product.updated and product.deleted.
31086: Custom topics can also be used which map to a single hook name, for example you could add a webhook with topic action.woocommerce_add_to_cart that is triggered on that event. Custom topics pass the first hook argument to the payload, so in this example the cart_item_key would be included in the payload.
31087: Delivery/payload
31088: Delivery is performed using wp_remote_post() (HTTP POST) and processed in the background by default using wp-cron. A few custom headers are added to the request to help the receiver process the webhook:
31089: X-WC-Webhook-Source: http://example.com/.
31090: X-WC-Webhook-Topic - e.g. order.updated.
31091: X-WC-Webhook-Resource - e.g. order.
31092: X-WC-Webhook-Event - e.g. updated.
31093: X-WC-Webhook-Signature - a base64 encoded HMAC-SHA256 hash of the payload.
31094: X-WC-Webhook-ID - webhook's post ID.
31095: X-WC-Webhook-Delivery-ID - delivery log ID (a comment).
31096: The payload is JSON encoded and for API resources (coupons, customers, orders, products), the response is exactly the same as if requested via the REST API.
31097: Logging
31098: Requests/responses are logged using the WooCommerce logging system. Each delivery log includes:
31099: Request duration.
31100: Request URL, method, headers, and body.
31101: Response Code, message, headers, and body.
31102: After 5 consecutive failed deliveries (as defined by a non HTTP 2xx response code), the webhook is disabled and must be edited via the REST API to re-enable.
31103: Delivery logs can be accessed in "WooCommerce" > "Status" > "Logs".
31104: Visual interface
31105: You can find the Webhooks interface going to "WooCommerce" > "Settings" > "Advanced" > "Webhooks", see our Visual Webhooks docs for more details.

35: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration
36: Introduction​
37: WooCommerce registers product and order abilities in WordPress. With the MCP Adapter plugin, AI clients can discover and run these store operations through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), subject to WordPress and WooCommerce permissions.
38: info
39: Developer Preview Notice
40: The MCP implementation in WooCommerce is currently in developer preview. Implementation details, APIs, and integration patterns may change in future releases as the feature matures.
41: Enabling MCP Integration​
42: WooCommerce always registers its abilities through the WordPress Abilities API; there is no WooCommerce setting to turn on. To make them available to MCP clients, install and activate the MCP Adapter plugin:
43: wp plugin install mcp-adapter --activate
44: WooCommerce does not bundle the MCP adapter.
45: Authentication and Security​
46: WordPress Application Password Requirements​
47: Remote HTTP connections authenticate using a WordPress username and an Application Password. Do not use your account password or a WooCommerce REST API key.
48: To create an Application Password:
49: In the WordPress dashboard, navigate to Users → Profile.
50: Under Application Passwords, enter a name for the MCP client.
51: Click Add New Application Password.
52: Copy the generated password and store it securely. WordPress only displays it once.
53: Use the WordPress username and generated password as WP_API_USERNAME and WP_API_PASSWORD in the remote proxy configuration. Application Passwords can be revoked independently from the user's profile.
54: HTTPS Enforcement​
55: Use HTTPS for remote HTTP connections so credentials are encrypted in transit. Local STDIO connections authenticate through WP-CLI using the configured --user and do not require an Application Password.
56: Permission Validation​
57: The MCP Adapter authenticates requests as the WordPress user associated with the Application Password. The default server requires an authenticated user with the read capability, and each WooCommerce ability also enforces its own permission callback. Use a dedicated WordPress user with only the capabilities the MCP client needs.
58: Server Endpoint​
59: WooCommerce abilities are available through the WordPress MCP Adapter's default server:
60: https://yourstore.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server
61: The WooCommerce-specific /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp endpoint was removed in WooCommerce 11.3. See Removed in WooCommerce 11.3.
62: Connecting to the MCP Server​
63: Choose a connection method based on where the WordPress site is running. For a detailed overview and application-specific instructions, see Connecting AI applications and the wordpress/mcp-adaptor repository.
64: Local Sites Using STDIO​
65: For a local WordPress installation, MCP clients can connect directly through the MCP Adapter's WP-CLI command. The client needs access to the WordPress files and a working WP-CLI installation.
66: JSON Configuration​
67: Add the following server to your MCP client configuration. Replace the WordPress path and user with values from your local environment:
68: {
69: "mcpServers": {
70: "woocommerce_store": {
71: "command": "wp",
72: "args": [
73: "--path=/path/to/your/wordpress/site",
74: "mcp-adapter",
75: "serve",
76: "--server=mcp-adapter-default-server",
77: "--user=admin"
78: ]
79: }
80: }
81: }
82: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and Cursor use the mcpServers property shown above. For VS Code, use servers instead.
83: Command-Line Configuration​
84: Claude Code users can add the same server from the command line:
85: claude mcp add woocommerce_store -- \
86: wp --path=/path/to/your/wordpress/site \
87: mcp-adapter serve \
88: --server=mcp-adapter-default-server \
89: --user=admin
90: You can verify the server directly with WP-CLI:
91: echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}' | \
92: wp --path=/path/to/your/wordpress/site \
93: mcp-adapter serve \
94: --server=mcp-adapter-default-server \
95: --user=admin
96: Remote Sites Using HTTP​
97: For a remote WordPress installation, use the @automattic/mcp-wordpress-remote proxy. The proxy translates the MCP client's local STDIO messages into HTTP requests to the WordPress MCP Adapter.
98: Before connecting:
99: Create or select a dedicated WordPress user with the minimum required capabilities.
100: Open the user's Profile screen and create a WordPress Application Password.
101: Confirm the site uses HTTPS and non-Plain permalinks.
102: JSON Configuration​
103: Add the following server to your MCP client configuration. Replace the example URL, username, and Application Password:
104: {
105: "mcpServers": {
106: "woocommerce_store": {
107: "command": "npx",
108: "args": [
109: "-y",
110: "@automattic/mcp-wordpress-remote@latest"
111: ],
112: "env": {
113: "WP_API_URL": "https://yourstore.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server",
114: "WP_API_USERNAME": "your-username",
115: "WP_API_PASSWORD": "your-application-password"
116: }
117: }
118: }
119: }
120: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and Cursor use the mcpServers property shown above. For VS Code, use servers instead. Do not commit a configuration containing an Application Password to version control.
121: Command-Line Configuration​
122: Claude Code users can add the remote server from the command line:
123: claude mcp add \
124: --env WP_API_URL=https://yourstore.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server \
125: --env WP_API_USERNAME=your-username \
126: --env WP_API_PASSWORD='your-application-password' \
127: woocommerce_store \
128: -- npx -y @automattic/mcp-wordpress-remote@latest
129: Troubleshooting: For common setup issues with npx versions or SSL in local environments, see the mcp-wordpress-remote troubleshooting guide.
130: Discover WooCommerce Abilities​
131: The default MCP server exposes three tools: mcp-adapter-discover-abilities, mcp-adapter-get-ability-info, and mcp-adapter-execute-ability. A tools/list response shows these adapter tools, not a separate tool for each WooCommerce ability. Use the discovery tool to list available abilities, then get an ability's schema before executing it.
132: For a local site, you can check discovery with WP-CLI:
133: echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"mcp-adapter-discover-abilities","arguments":{}}}' | \
134: wp --path=/path/to/your/wordpress/site \
135: mcp-adapter serve \
136: --server=mcp-adapter-default-server \
137: --user=admin
138: On a WooCommerce 11.3 site, the response should include abilities such as woocommerce/products-query and woocommerce/order-notes-query. Each ability checks permissions when it runs. See the MCP Adapter default server guide for the discovery and execution flow.
139: Background​
140: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI applications to securely connect to external data sources and tools. Using MCP with WooCommerce relies on two core technologies:
141: WordPress Abilities API - A standardized system for registering capabilities in WordPress, included in WordPress core
142: WordPress MCP Adapter - The core MCP protocol implementation, installed as the MCP Adapter plugin
143: This architecture allows WooCommerce to expose operations as MCP tools through the flexible WordPress Abilities system while maintaining existing security and permission models.
144: What's Available​
145: WooCommerce registers purpose-built abilities for core store operations. These abilities are available through the WordPress Abilities API and can be surfaced through the shared WordPress MCP adapter.
146: Purpose-Built WooCommerce Abilities​
147: Product Management​
148: Query products with filtering and pagination
149: Create new products
150: Update existing products
151: Delete products
152: Order Management​
153: Query orders with filtering and pagination
154: Query notes for an order (woocommerce/order-notes-query)
155: Update order status
156: Add order notes
157: All operations respect WooCommerce's existing permission system. MCP clients authenticate through the MCP Adapter as a WordPress user.
158: Removed in WooCommerce 11.3​
159: WooCommerce 11.3 removed the deprecated WooCommerce MCP endpoint and everything that only existed to support it:
160: The /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp endpoint and its WooCommerce REST API key authentication (X-MCP-API-Key). Requests to the endpoint now return HTTP 410 with a JSON-RPC error that explains how to connect through the MCP Adapter.
161: The REST-derived product and order abilities (woocommerce/products-list, woocommerce/orders-get, and similar), along with the woocommerce_mcp_include_ability, woocommerce_mcp_allow_insecure_transport, and woocommerce_check_rest_ability_permissions_for_method filters and the expose_in_deprecated_woocommerce_mcp ability metadata.
162: Custom abilities registered by extensions or custom code that appeared in the removed endpoint don't carry over automatically. Before WooCommerce 10.9, the endpoint included abilities in the woocommerce/ namespace; from 10.9, it included abilities with expose_in_deprecated_woocommerce_mcp set to true; and the woocommerce_mcp_include_ability filter could add or remove abilities in either version. The MCP Adapter's default server ignores all of these. It only exposes an ability when its meta.mcp.public is true (if meta.mcp.public is not set, the adapter falls back to the top-level meta.public). To keep a custom ability available to MCP clients, set that metadata as shown in Adding Custom Abilities.
163: To keep using WooCommerce with MCP, install the MCP Adapter plugin and connect your MCP client to its default server, as described in Connecting to the MCP Server. Stores that had the WooCommerce MCP feature enabled see an admin notice about the change.
164: warning
165: Data Privacy Notice
166: Order and customer operations may expose personally identifiable information (PII) including names, email addresses, physical addresses, and payment details. You are responsible for ensuring compliance with applicable data protection regulations. Connect MCP clients as a dedicated WordPress user with only the capabilities they need, revoke Application Passwords you no longer use, and follow your organization's data retention and handling policies.
167: Architecture​
168: Data Flow Overview​
169: The MCP integration uses a multi-layered architecture to bridge between MCP clients and WordPress:
170: AI Client (Claude, etc.)
171: ↓ (MCP protocol over stdio/JSON-RPC)
172: Local MCP Proxy (mcp-wordpress-remote)
173: ↓ (HTTP/HTTPS requests with authentication)
174: Remote WordPress MCP Server (mcp-adapter)
175: ↓ (WordPress Abilities API)
176: WooCommerce Abilities
177: ↓ (REST API calls or direct operations)
178: WooCommerce Core
179: Architecture Components​
180: Local MCP Proxy (mcp-wordpress-remote)
181: Runs locally on the developer's machine as a Node.js process
182: Converts MCP protocol messages to HTTP requests
183: Handles authentication header injection
184: Bridges the protocol gap between MCP clients and WordPress REST endpoints
185: Remote WordPress MCP Server (mcp-adapter)
186: Is provided by the MCP Adapter plugin, which must be installed and active
187: Powers MCP tool discovery and execution for WordPress abilities
188: WordPress Abilities System​
189: Provides a standardized way to register and execute capabilities
190: Acts as an abstraction layer between MCP tools and actual operations
191: Enables flexible implementation approaches (direct operations, REST bridging, and so on)
192: Core Components​
193: Purpose-Built Domain Abilities (Domain)
194: Provide WooCommerce product and order abilities backed by domain APIs
195: Use shared WordPress MCP adapter metadata (mcp.public and mcp.type) for MCP exposure
196: Keep the ability contract focused on agent-friendly store operations
197: Implementation Approach​
198: WooCommerce implements its abilities as purpose-built domain abilities. These abilities use schemas and response shapes designed for agent workflows instead of automatically projecting every REST-shaped operation into MCP.
199: Extending MCP Capabilities​
200: Third-party plugins can register additional abilities using the WordPress Abilities API. Abilities can be implemented in various ways, including direct operations, custom logic, REST endpoint bridging, or external integrations.
201: Adding Custom Abilities​
202: Register an ability category first, then register the ability during the WordPress Abilities API init hook:
203: add_action( 'wp_abilities_api_categories_init', function() {
204: if ( ! function_exists( 'wp_register_ability_category' ) ) {
205: return;
206: }
207: if ( function_exists( 'wp_has_ability_category' ) && wp_has_ability_category( 'your-plugin' ) ) {
208: return;
209: }
210: wp_register_ability_category(
211: 'your-plugin',
212: array(
213: 'label' => __( 'Your Plugin', 'your-plugin' ),
214: 'description' => __( 'Abilities provided by Your Plugin.', 'your-plugin' ),
215: )
216: );
217: });
218: add_action( 'wp_abilities_api_init', function() {
219: if ( ! function_exists( 'wp_register_ability' ) ) {
220: return;
221: }
222: wp_register_ability(
223: 'your-plugin/custom-operation',
224: array(
225: 'label' => __( 'Custom Store Operation', 'your-plugin' ),
226: 'description' => __( 'Performs a custom store operation.', 'your-plugin' ),
227: 'category' => 'your-plugin',
228: 'execute_callback' => 'your_custom_ability_handler',
229: 'permission_callback' => function () {
230: return current_user_can( 'manage_woocommerce' );
231: },
232: 'input_schema' => array(
233: 'type' => 'object',
234: 'properties' => array(
235: 'store_id' => array(
236: 'type' => 'integer',
237: 'description' => 'Store identifier',
238: ),
239: ),
240: 'required' => array( 'store_id' ),
241: ),
242: 'output_schema' => array(
243: 'type' => 'object',
244: 'properties' => array(
245: 'success' => array(
246: 'type' => 'boolean',
247: 'description' => 'Operation result',
248: ),
249: ),
250: ),
251: 'meta' => array(
252: 'show_in_rest' => true,
253: 'mcp' => array(
254: 'public' => true,
255: 'type' => 'tool',
256: ),
257: ),
258: )
259: );
260: });
261: The mcp.public and mcp.type metadata tells the shared WordPress MCP adapter that the ability can be exposed as an MCP tool. The show_in_rest metadata exposes the ability through the Abilities API REST routes.
262: Development Example​
263: For a complete working example, see the WooCommerce MCP Ability Demo Plugin. This demonstration plugin shows how third-party developers can:
264: Register custom abilities using the WordPress Abilities API
265: Define comprehensive input and output schemas
266: Implement proper permission handling
267: Integrate with MCP through the shared WordPress MCP adapter
268: The demo plugin creates a woocommerce-demo/store-info ability that retrieves store information and statistics, demonstrating the integration patterns for extending WooCommerce MCP capabilities while using a direct implementation approach rather than REST endpoint bridging.
269: Troubleshooting​
270: Common Issues​
271: MCP Server Not Available​
272: Verify the MCP Adapter plugin is installed and active
273: Confirm the client connects to /wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server, not the removed /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp endpoint
274: Authentication Failures​
275: Confirm WP_API_USERNAME matches the WordPress user that created the Application Password
276: Confirm WP_API_PASSWORD contains an active Application Password, not the user's account password or a WooCommerce REST API key
277: Verify the WordPress user has the capabilities required by the ability
278: Ensure HTTPS is used for remote HTTP connections
279: Ability Not Found​
280: Confirm the ability category is registered during wp_abilities_api_categories_init
281: Confirm abilities are registered during wp_abilities_api_init
282: Verify ability callbacks are accessible
283: Check WooCommerce → Status → Logs for entries with source woocommerce-abilities.
284: Important Considerations​
285: Developer Preview: This feature is in preview status and may change
286: Implementation Approach: WooCommerce uses purpose-built domain abilities
287: Breaking Changes: Future updates may introduce breaking changes
288: Production Testing: Thoroughly test before deploying to production
289: API Stability: The WordPress Abilities API and MCP adapter are evolving

231: WooCommerce Monorepo
232: Welcome to the WooCommerce monorepo on GitHub. Here you can find all of the plugins, packages, and tools used in the development of the core WooCommerce plugin as well as WooCommerce extensions. You can browse the source, look at open issues, contribute code, and keep track of ongoing development.
233: We recommend all developers follow the WooCommerce development blog to stay up to date with everything happening in the project. You can also follow @DevelopWoo on X (formerly Twitter) for the latest development updates.
234: Getting Started
235: To get up and running within the WooCommerce Monorepo, you will need to make sure that you have installed all of the prerequisites.
236: Prerequisites
237: Node.js: Required to run PNPM and the monorepo's build and test scripts. Use the Node version pinned in package.json (devEngines.runtime, mirrored in .nvmrc); PNPM fails with an error when you run it on a different version. A Node version manager such as NVM is optional, but still handy for installing Node itself.
238: PNPM: Our repository utilizes PNPM to manage project dependencies and run various scripts involved in building and testing projects.
239: PHP 7.4+: WooCommerce Core currently requires PHP version 7.4 or higher. It is also needed to run Composer and various project build scripts. See troubleshooting for troubleshooting problems installing PHP.
240: Composer: We use Composer to manage all of the dependencies for PHP packages and plugins.
241: Note: A POSIX-compliant operating system (e.g., Linux, macOS) is assumed. If you're working on a Windows machine, the recommended approach is to use WSL (available since Windows 10).
242: Once you've installed all prerequisites, the following will prepare all of the build outputs necessary for development:
243: # Install the PHP and Composer dependencies for all of the plugins, packages, and tools.
244: # PNPM fails with an error when the Node version differs from the pinned one (see Prerequisites).
245: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
246: # Build all of the plugins, packages, and tools in the monorepo
247: pnpm build
248: Repository Structure
249: Each plugin, package, and tool has its own package.json file containing project-specific dependencies and scripts. Most projects also contain a README.md file with any project-specific setup instructions and documentation.
250: Plugins: Our repository contains plugins that relate to or otherwise aid in the development of WooCommerce.
251: WooCommerce Core: The core WooCommerce plugin is available in the plugins directory.
252: Packages: Contained within the packages directory are all of the PHP and JavaScript provided for the community. Some of these are internal dependencies and are marked with an internal- prefix.
253: Tools: We also have a growing number of tools within our repository. Many of these are intended to be utilities and scripts for use in the monorepo, but, this directory may also contain external tools.
254: If you'd like to learn more about how our monorepo works, please check out this guide here.
255: Reporting Security Issues
256: To disclose a security issue to our team, please submit a report via HackerOne here.
257: Support
258: This repository is not suitable for support. Please don't use our issue tracker for support requests, but for core WooCommerce issues only. Support can take place through the appropriate channels:
259: If you have a problem, you may want to start with the self help guide.
260: The WooCommerce.com premium support portal for customers who have purchased themes or extensions.
261: Our community forum on wp.org which is available for all WooCommerce users.
262: The Official WooCommerce Facebook Group.
263: For customizations, you may want to check our list of WooExperts or Codeable.
264: NOTE: Unfortunately, we are unable to honor support requests in issues on this repository; as a result, any requests submitted in this manner will be closed.
265: Community
266: For peer to peer support, real-time announcements, and office hours, please join our slack community!
267: Contributing to WooCommerce
268: As an open-source project, we rely on community contributions to continue to improve WooCommerce. To get started, check out our Contributing guide for a quick reference of common development commands, or visit the Contributing to Woo docs for broader contribution guidelines.

59: This page is for Developer.
60: BigCommerce offers a suite of APIs that let you manage store data, sign customers in, make client-side queries for product information, and write apps that integrate third-party services into store operations.
61: BigCommerce API accounts play a role in every authenticated request to our servers. Our API accounts come in a few different flavors to meet the needs of different use cases. For example, app API accounts work well in multi-store contexts, whereas store API accounts are a good choice for frontend applications. Some endpoints only work with one kind of API account.
62: For an overview of the authentication schemes that our APIs use, see the Authentication section below.
63: API accounts
64: BigCommerce offers three types of OAuth-based API accounts to developers who wish to use BigCommerce’s REST APIs: store-level credentials, app-level credentials, and account-level credentials. This section describes the difference between the three, how to obtain and revoke account credentials, and the use cases for each. It also contains a reference for available OAuth scopes and provides a compelling list of reasons to migrate from legacy API tokens to OAuth credentials.
65: Every parent set of API credentials that you request for your store is its own API account. At its simplest, an API account consists of the following:
66: The client_id uniquely identifies the app or user, or the client, making a request.
67: The client_secret is a cryptographically secure value known only to the client and BigCommerce.
68: Every active API account has at least one access_token. Store-level API accounts include a static access token that does not change. App-level API accounts expect each application to generate a unique access token for every store that installs the app. Account-level API accounts include a single access token that belongs to the parent account of the store that the user is signed in to at the time of creation.
69: Guard these values closely. The client ID and client secret will never change; access tokens do not expire based on time and cannot be manually invalidated. It’s best practice to limit each account’s OAuth scope to only the privileges needed to complete that app or user’s designated tasks. Create separate API accounts for each app, store API user or function, or account-related implementation.
70: Choosing the right kind of API account
71: Where both types of API account are supported, review the preceding sections to make an informed choice about which best fits your use case.
72: API or Use CaseStore-level API accountApp-level API accountAccount-level API account
73: GraphQL Account API, including Users×

75: GraphQL Storefront API×

77: REST Store Management APIs××
78: REST Storefront API×
