87: Store-level API accounts
88: Merchants generate single-store API credentials when they create API accounts in their store control panel, in the Settings > Store-level API accounts menu. Use these credentials to read and change one store’s data with BigCommerce’s APIs. You can’t change store-level access tokens or OAuth scopes.
89: In addition to the API account components in the preceding section, store-level API accounts contain the following attributes out of the box:
90: An access_token, which accompanies most REST API requests.
91: The client name is a label for your convenience, and it doesn’t accompany requests.
92: The API path is the URL to which you make requests. The API path won’t change, but it will have /v3/ or /v2/ appended to it, depending on the current version for the endpoint you’re querying.
93: Most APIs that work with store-level API accounts use the access_token to authenticate requests to BigCommerce. However, a few use the access token to generate a temporary credential. To learn more about special cases that involve store-level credentials, consult the documentation for the API you want to use.
94: Be careful with client secrets
95: Do not send your client_secret or access_token in plain text or an unencrypted payload. Be particularly careful with the client_secret. An attacker can use your client_secret to both sign and decrypt JWTs sent between you and BigCommerce.
96: Creating store-level API credentials
97: To create a store-level API account, consult our Knowledge Base article on Creating a Store API Account.
98: Revoking store-level API credentials
99: To revoke store-level API credentials, you must delete the corresponding store API account. If the client_id and client_secret are compromised, or the account has become unnecessary, secure your account by deleting the API account. You cannot recover a deleted API account, so take care.
100: Delete carefully
101: Deleting an account cannot be undone, so be sure before clicking the trash can icon. You can also use the checkboxes on the left side to delete multiple accounts at once – but be especially careful when using this option.
102: To delete a store-level API account, consult our Knowledge Base article on Deleting a Store API Account.
103: Don’t forget your webhooks and metafields
104: Some resources are only accessible to the API account that created them. These include webhooks, metafields, and scripts. If you need to revoke a store-level API account, plan accordingly.
105: Webhooks do not persist upon account deletion. Verify webhooks associated with an account before deleting it.
106: App-level API accounts
107: You can create app-level API accounts in the Developer Portal. After a store owner or authorized user installs and authorizes an app, most apps use access tokens generated from the API account’s client ID, client secret, and a temporary grant code to read and change store data. Generate access tokens with the BigCommerce-initiated grant code authorization flow.
108: Some APIs use app-level API accounts to implement alternative authentication patterns. For a summary of all our authentication methods, see the authentication schemes described earlier in this article.
109: For more on working with apps, see our Guide to Building Apps. The sections on Implementing OAuth and Callback Handlers are particularly relevant to generating access tokens.
110: Creating app-level API credentials
111: To create an app and its associated API account, consult our article on Managing Apps in the Developer Portal.
112: App-level access tokens
113: App-level API accounts do not come pre-configured with an access token. Each time a store installs your app, BigCommerce initiates a grant code authorization flow to help your app generate a dedicated access token for that store. For further details, see Authenticating an app.
114: Revoking app-level API credentials
115: There is no way to manually revoke or force-regenerate app-level API account access tokens. However, either of the following actions triggers a token refresh:
116: When the store owner’s email address changes
117: When you modify the app API account’s OAuth scopes
118: After one of these changes, the store owner will be prompted to review the change and reauthorize the app the next time they click the app icon in the store control panel.
119: Delete apps carefully
120: When you delete an app in the Dev Portal, there is no way to recover the client ID or client secret. If you choose to do this, don’t forget to mitigate the potential loss of webhook and metafield-related data and functionality.
121: To delete an app-level API account, consult our article on Managing Apps in the Developer Portal.
122: Account-level API accounts
123: Account-level API accounts are designed to work with the GraphQL Account API, which manages resources beyond the scope of a single store. For example, managing control panel users in the BigCommerce ecosystem. Current and future features available using the GraphQL Account API toolset allow developers to build custom integrations and solutions that require high-level access to store and platform resources. Using this API, you can integrate with third-party applications, streamline and automate business processes, and manage multiple merchant stores per account.
124: Creating account-level credentials
125: To create an account-level API account visit the account control panel or the store control panel for a member store at Settings > Account-level API accounts.
126: To learn more about creating an account-level API account, consult our Knowledge Base article on API Accounts.
127: When you create account-level credentials, they belong to the parent account for the store you’re signed in to.
128: Account-level API credentials provide direct access to all the account’s stores, not just the store that was signed in at the time of creation. Their permissions are limited only by the OAuth scopes they were granted at the time of creation. Keep the access token and client secret secure.
129: Revoking account-level API credentials
130: An account-level access token is valid until the account is no longer active. However, you can manually delete account-level credentials.
131: Deleting API accounts is risky and must be done with caution. Only users who have the correct permissions can perform this action.
132: To delete an account-level API account, visit the account control panel and find the account you want to delete in the list. Click the three dots in the Action column, then click Delete. Follow any prompts that appear.
133: Migrating from legacy to OAuth
134: Legacy API Accounts
135: BigCommerce no longer issues legacy API Accounts to new stores. Existing legacy API Accounts will continue to work until further notice. Migrate to OAuth as soon as possible.
136: Benefits of migrating to OAuth
137: We recommend migrating from legacy API credentials to OAuth, if you haven’t already. Migration provides a wealth of benefits, including the following:
138: Unified requests: Send all OAuth requests to a single URL: https://api.bigcommerce.com. Using a common hostname prevents interruptions of service when a store’s domain or SSL/TLS certificate changes or expires.
139: Latest and greatest APIs: BigCommerce’s V3 APIs are accessible exclusively with OAuth.
140: Webhook subscriptions: OAuth API accounts can subscribe to real-time event notifications using BigCommerce’s webhooks.
141: Shared secrets: Use new APIs and endpoints that require shared secrets, including the Customer Login and Current Customer APIs.
142: Zippier responses: Responses to OAuth requests use gzip compression and less of your bandwidth.
143: Better security with granular permissions: All OAuth tokens are scoped to specific operations and endpoints. If you suspect a breach, you will know which resources could be affected.
144: How to migrate
145: Before you update your API connections to use OAuth instead of legacy basic authentication, take the following actions:
146: Create an API account appropriate to your use case. Keeping in mind the API endpoints your connections use, create either a store API account or an app API account per the preceding instructions. To adhere to industry-standard security practices, configure the account with the minimum OAuth scopes for your use case. If you’re using an app API account, you can always modify the scope later.
147: If you use one of our client libraries, consult the library’s documentation for establishing an optimal OAuth configuration.
148: After you create your connection, update your connection parameters as follows:
149: Use https://api.bigcommerce.com as the gateway URL instead of the BigCommerce store’s secure hostname. For example, route requests that formerly went to https://store-{{store_hash}}.mybigcommerce.com/api/v2/orders/{{order_id}} or https://my-custom-store-domain.com/api/v2/orders/{{order_id}} will now use https://api.bigcommerce.com/stores/{{store_hash}}/v2/orders/{{order_id}}.
150: Rewrite your HTTP request headers to use the X-Auth-Token header to pass the API account’s access_token instead of the Authorization header. For more information, see the access tokens section above.
151: Rate limiting works differently for OAuth API connections. For details, see the Rate Limits section of our API best practices article.
152: OAuth scopes
153: Scope grants and limits a program’s ability to read and write data. Set the scopes to the minimum level of access your implementation needs.
154: All OAuth scopes except default provide read-only permissions scopes so that you can limit some accounts to sending GET and HEAD requests.
155: Webhooks are accessible from the default scope that is automatically accessible to all API accounts.

251: Authentication
252: This section provides an overview of the authentication schemes that our APIs use, organized by the header or other mechanism they use to authenticate with our servers.
253: Stable tokens
254: Most of our APIs use credentials that do not expire based on a time frame. Depending on the type of API account the credentials belong to, they might expire based on user or developer actions.
255: The following sections describe the two authentication schemes we use that rely on stable tokens. They include example requests and list or describe the endpoints to which the schemes apply.
256: Access tokens
257: Legacy API accounts used HTTP basic authentication. They are no longer available to new stores. For more information, see API Accounts: Migrating from legacy to OAuth.
258: Most of our REST endpoints and GraphQL Admin API endpoints use the X-Auth-Token header to authenticate to BigCommerce servers. For more about the APIs that do NOT use the X-Auth-Token header, consult this article’s sections on dynamic tokens and same-origin CORS authentication.
259: The X-Auth-Token header uses access tokens to authenticate requests. Create an OAuth API account to generate access tokens. Pass the access token as the value of the X-Auth-Token header of the request you want to authenticate.
260: The B2B REST Management API also uses the X-Auth-Token header, but requires the additional X-Store-Hash header to identify the store. B2B REST Management API endpoints use a different base URL (https://api-b2b.bigcommerce.com), so the store hash is not included in the request path as it is for other BigCommerce REST APIs. For more on B2B authentication, see Authentication for hosted storefronts.
261: The X-Auth-Client header is deprecated
262: Your API account’s client ID is no longer a required header value.
263: For a request to succeed, the access token’s API account must have permission to receive the response. Configure your API account with the minimum set of OAuth scopes that your implementation needs.
264: To find the specific OAuth scopes your requests require, consult the root API reference pages for the families of endpoints you plan to use. For example, see the OAuth scopes for the Email Templates endpoints. We also maintain a list of all our OAuth scopes.

276: Client ID
277: Another stable token-based scheme involves mutual authentication. The requesting app identifies itself by sending an API account’s client ID as a query parameter, and our servers return a BigCommerce-generated JSON web token, or JWT, which securely encrypts merchant data. The app can decode the JWT to view the response. For example, the Current Customer API’s JWT payload identifies the currently signed-in customer.

301: Dynamic tokens
302: Several of our APIs authenticate with JSON web tokens, or JWTs. JWTs authorize both the requester and the recipient because they contain a signed payload that the recipient must successfully decrypt before working with the transmitted data. You can use some JWTs for any number of requests within an expiration window; others must be unique to each request.
303: Our JWT-based authentication schemes fall into the following categories:
304: The user passes a BigCommerce-generated JWT as part of the value of the Authorization header
305: The user sends BigCommerce a user-generated JWT
306: BigCommerce-encrypted payload JWTs send apps information as part of a signed JWT’s payload
307: All requests that use JWTs require at least two steps. In addition to the request itself, you must also either get, make, or decrypt the JWT that the request sends or receives. The following sections describe the steps for these three JWT-based authentication schemes, reference the endpoints to which they apply, and give example requests.
308: Make sure your tokens are in scope
309: Before you create an API account to request dynamic tokens, determine the required OAuth scopes by consulting the documentation for your target endpoint and its corresponding REST token generation endpoint.
310: BigCommerce-generated JWTs
311: Some APIs authenticate with an Authorization header that contains a string concatenated with a BigCommerce-generated JWT. Requests to these APIs contain the following two parts:
312: The user obtains the JWT by:
313: Making an API request to BigCommerce, or
314: On Stencil storefronts, extracting it from the page’s context.
315: The user sends the intended request.

364: BigCommerce-encrypted payload JWTs
365: BigCommerce-encrypted payload JWTs let control panel apps listen to and reason about events that affect them, but happen outside the app itself. These events include users installing, loading, and uninstalling the app. Working with these JWTs includes the following parts:
366: The app receives the JWT from BigCommerce
367: The app validates the JWT, then decrypts its payload
368: The payload’s data informs what the app does next
369: To learn more, see our Apps Guide, especially the articles on authorization, installation, and other app callback events.
370: Same-origin CORS authentication
371: The following APIs rely on CORS headers for authentication. You do not need to send any BigCommerce-specific tokens with your requests to these endpoints.
372: REST Storefront API
373: The REST Storefront API lets you make client-side requests for carts, checkouts, and orders using JavaScript or an alternative language that compiles to run in the browser. It is a convenience collection of operations that affect one customer at a time and run in the context of the customer’s current session on a BigCommerce-hosted storefront. You can perform authenticated versions of the same operations using the GraphQL Storefront API or the REST Store Management APIs.
374: The following examples illustrate how to make calls to the REST Storefront API:
375: Example script: REST Storefront API call
376: const storefrontCall = (endpoint, requestBody = null) => {
377: let resource = `${window.location.origin}/api/storefront${endpoint.route}`;
378: let init = {
379: method: endpoint.method,
380: credentials: "same-origin",
381: headers: {
382: // note: no authorization
383: "Accept": endpoint.accept,
384: }
385: }
386: if(requestBody) {
387: init.body = JSON.stringify(requestBody);
388: init.headers["Content-Type"] = endpoint.content;
389: }
390: return fetch(resource, init)
391: .then(response => {
392: console.log(response);
393: if(response.status === endpoint.success) {
394: // resolve promise using the Fetch API method that correlates with the endpoint.accept value
395: return response.json(); // or response.text()
396: } else {
397: return new Error(`response.status is ${response.status}`);
398: }
399: })
400: .then(result => {
401: console.log(result); // requested data
402: // do stuff...
403: })
404: .catch(error => console.error(error));
405: }

22: Create a Sandbox Store
23: Copy page
24: This page is for Developer.
25: Sandbox stores are intended for developing and testing apps. They cannot process any live transactions.
26: This article walks you through the steps of creating a sandbox store and explains how to open a support case if you encounter any issues.
27: Creating a sandbox store
28: To create a sandbox store, complete the following steps:
29: Navigate to the BigCommerce Partner Portal and sign in using your credentials.
30: After signing in, hover over Create New in the top navigation, then select one of the following two options:
31: To register a new deal and create an associated sandbox, select Deal Registration and consult the following instructions to create a Deal Registration sandbox.
32: To create a sandbox for your own general use, select Partner Use Sandbox and consult the following instructions to create a Partner Sandbox.
33: Store regions are immutable
34: You cannot update the store region of a partner sandbox.
35: Deal Registration sandbox
36: After you click Create New > Deal Registration in the top navigation, complete the following steps:
37: On the Create a Store/Register a Deal page, complete all the required fields.
38: To ensure that your Deal Registration also includes a sandbox store, locate the Create a Store? field, then select Partner Sandbox.
39: In the Store Region field, select the global region of best fit for your use case.
40: Below the Create a Store? field, select the checkbox to acknowledge that the Store Region value cannot be changed.
41: Click Submit.
42: After you click Submit, you will receive two emails:
43: a Deal Registration confirmation email, and
44: an email that contains sign in credentials for the new sandbox.
45: For more about viewing and working with partner sandboxes, consult the following section on accessing and managing partner sandboxes.
46: Partner Use sandbox
47: After you click Create New > Partner Use Sandbox in the top navigation, complete the following steps:
48: On the Create a Partner Sandbox page, give the sandbox a name.
49: In the Store Region field, select the global region of best fit for your use case.
50: Below the Store Region field, select the checkbox to acknowledge that the store region cannot be changed.
51: Click Submit.
52: After you click Submit, you will receive an email that contains sign in credentials for the new sandbox.
53: For more about viewing and working with partner sandboxes, consult the following section on accessing and managing partner sandboxes.
54: Accessing and managing partner sandboxes
55: Allow up to 15 minutes for the new store to appear in any list of stores.
56: The email that contains the sandbox credentials is sent only once. However, you can access the sandbox by signing in to the BigCommerce account that uses the same email address as your Partner Portal account.
57: To review and manage your sandbox and trial stores in the Partner Portal, hover over Reporting in the top navigation, then click Review Sandboxes & Trials.
58: Creating a support case
59: If you encounter trouble creating or managing partner sandboxes, you can create a partner-specific support case.
60: To create a partner-specific support case, complete the following steps:
61: Sign in to the Partner Portal.
62: In the top navigation, hover over Support, then click Contact Support.
63: On the Contact Support page, click the Create a Support Case card.
64: Indicate whether you need Product Support or Billing Support.
65: When asked Is this related to a specific store?; answer Yes.
66: Enter the canonical URL of your sandbox store. For example, https://store-xxxxxxxxx.mybigcommerce.com.
67: Sign in to the BigCommerce account that uses the same email address as your Partner Portal account.
68: At the bottom of the Admin panel, click Help, then locate the Services & Support section to connect with our support team using your desired mode of communication.

384: Frequently asked questions
385: Do you offer a free trial?
386: Yes, we offer a fully functional 15-day free trial, during which you can test drive BigCommerce and build your site. You don't need a credit card to sign up; there's no obligation and no risk.
387: Can I launch a store and complete transactions during my trial?
388: Yes, our 15-day free trial is a fully-functional product that would allow you to launch a store and take payments. You will need to set up a payments partner to accept payments and complete transactions.
389: What happens to my store at the end of my trial?
390: We’ll send you a reminder to upgrade your store at the end of your free trial. If you choose not to upgrade, we’ll keep your data for 90 days — just choose a subscription plan to get your store up and running again. During this time, your customers won’t be able to access your store, and you’ll only be able to log in to choose a plan. After 90 days, your store will be automatically deleted, and we’ll no longer be able to restore it.
391: Are there any contracts to sign?
392: Our Core, Growth, and Scale plans don’t require a contract, and you can cancel at any time in the control panel. If you do, we’ll stop billing you immediately. Contracts are available for BigCommerce’s Performance plan to ensure we’re meeting the level of service that your business needs.
393: How do automatic upgrades work?
394: BigCommerce plans are based on your trailing twelve-month (TTM) GMV. As your sales grow and exceed your plan’s threshold (for example, $30K on Core or $100K on Growth), you’ll be notified and automatically upgraded to the next plan to support your growth. On higher tiers like Scale and Performance, there are no abrupt jumps or block charges — instead, a continuous overage rate applies only to orders above your plan’s limit (GMV or orders). This means you can grow without hitting hard limits, while maintaining predictable, incremental costs.
395: What transactions count toward my trailing 12 months of sales/orders?
396: Eligible sales include product price (net of any discounts), as well as taxes and shipping. Social commerce transactions from Pinterest, Facebook, and Twitter, and native marketplace integrations (specifically, eBay and Amazon) count as sales/orders. BigCommerce uses GMV, your gross order value after a 10% reduction, to evaluate plan thresholds. Learn more about BigCommerce pricing.﻿
397: How do I change my plan?

Based on your plan, you may be eligible for that plan’s published processing rate. Eligibility requires that you must be a United States-based business. Then,
414: ﻿
415: (1) If you are a new BigCommerce Merchant using a trial PayPal Braintree account, you will need to select a qualifying BigCommerce Plan (Growth, Scale, or Performance). Go into your BigCommerce account Client Area and accept the terms of the selected BigCommerce plan and establish a billing agreement. You will then be charged the first month’s fee for your BigCommerce plan, and you will become eligible to apply for the negotiated payment processing rates with PayPal Braintree. If you are an existing BigCommerce Merchant already in a Growth, Scale, or Performance plan, you do not need to complete this step.
416: (2) From within the BigCommerce account Control Panel Payment Settings area, complete and submit the PayPal Braintree application to upgrade from a trial to a full account. Additional information may be requested from the PayPal Braintree team during the process of reviewing your application.
417: (3) 2 to 3 business days following your approval* for a PayPal Braintree account, you will be emailed a Pricing Contract to digitally sign. We suggest adding echosign@echosign.com to your email whitelist to reduce the risk of it going to your spam folder. Follow the instructions in the email on how to sign and return the contract.
418: (4) Your account will then be updated to reflect the new rate, and you will receive a notification email with the updated rate, which can take up to 10 business days. Your new rate will only apply to transactions after the date on your notification email.

312: The documentation site serves two versions:

316: API Documentation
317: API documentation is auto-generated from JSDoc comments in the @salesforce/b2c-tooling-sdk package. The entry points are defined in typedoc.json:
318: See the documentation site for the generated API reference.
319: auth - Authentication strategies (OAuth, API Key, Basic)
320: instance - B2C instance configuration
321: platform - MRT and ODS clients
322: operations/code - Cartridge code operations
323: operations/jobs - Job execution
324: operations/sites - Site management
325: i18n - Internationalization utilities
326: logging - Structured logging
327: When adding new public APIs, ensure they have comprehensive JSDoc comments as these will appear in the generated documentation.
328: Bundled Platform Data (Script API docs, schemas, job steps)
329: The SDK ships several corpora derived from the B2C Commerce platform under packages/b2c-tooling-sdk/data/:
330: Directory
331: Contents
332: Consumed by
333: script-api/
334: Script API reference markdown + search index
335: b2c docs search / docs read, MCP docs_*
336: content-schemas/
337: Page Designer / content metadefinition JSON schemas
338: b2c content validate
339: xsd/
340: Import/export XSD schemas + search index
341: b2c docs schema *, b2c validate, MCP validate_xml_schema
342: xml-validator/
343: libxml2 compiled to WebAssembly; built by wasm/xml-validator/build.sh and verified in CI
344: b2c validate, MCP validate_xml_schema
345: job-steps/
346: Standard job-step markdown + dataset + search index
347: b2c docs search / docs read
348: All of these originate from the same documentation archive that b2c docs download fetches from an instance (the inner DWAPP-<version>-API-doc.zip). To refresh all of them to a new platform release at once, run the maintainer script against a current instance (it uses your default instance/auth via the CLI):
349: # Refresh every data set and regenerate the derived indexes
350: pnpm --filter @salesforce/b2c-tooling-sdk run refresh:docs-data
351: # Target a non-default instance, or keep the temp workdir for inspection
352: B2C_INSTANCE=my-sandbox KEEP_WORKDIR=1 pnpm --filter @salesforce/b2c-tooling-sdk run refresh:docs-data
353: The script prints the detected platform version (e.g. DWAPP 26.7). Afterward, review the diff under packages/b2c-tooling-sdk/data/ (index files always change their generatedAt timestamp; look for substantive schema/doc changes), run pnpm --filter @salesforce/b2c-tooling-sdk run test:agent, and add a changeset if the refresh changes user-facing behavior. See the sdk-module-development skill for details.
354: Releases and Publishing
355: This project uses Changesets for version management and publishes to npm using OIDC trusted publishers.
356: Release Type
357: npm Tag
358: Trigger
359: Stable
360: @latest
361: Merge version PR on main
362: Release Branch
363: @latest or @release-X.Y
364: Push to release/** branch
365: Nightly
366: @nightly
367: Manual
368: For detailed information about the release process, including release branches, see PUBLISHING.md.
369: Quick Reference
370: # Create a changeset for your changes
371: pnpm changeset
372: # Check pending changesets
373: pnpm changeset status
374: Preview Releases
375: Preview releases are available as tgz files on GitHub Releases for testing before npm publication.
376: Package Exports
377: The @salesforce/b2c-tooling-sdk package uses the exports field in package.json to define its public API surface. Each module is available as a subpath export:
378: import {OAuthStrategy} from '@salesforce/b2c-tooling-sdk/auth';
379: import {B2CInstance} from '@salesforce/b2c-tooling-sdk/instance';
380: import {getLogger} from '@salesforce/b2c-tooling-sdk/logging';
381: The development condition in exports enables direct TypeScript source resolution when using --conditions=development, which is how bin/dev.js works for local development.
382: Contributing
383: We welcome contributions! Please see our Contributing Guide for details on how to get started, submit pull requests, and our code of conduct.
384: Third-Party Dependency Review
385: To prevent net-new third-party libraries from being added without discussion, PRs are checked by the 3PL Guard workflow (Net-new 3PL check).
386: The check compares changed package.json files in the PR and detects net-new external dependencies.
387: If net-new dependencies are found, the PR is labeled needs-3pl-review and the check fails.
388: After discussion and approval, a maintainer adds the 3pl-approved label to allow the check to pass.
389: If the net-new dependency is removed, needs-3pl-review is removed automatically.
390: To enforce this as a merge gate, keep Net-new 3PL check as a required status check in branch protection.

1: REST API Overview
2: REST API Overview
3: The REST API documentation describes the REST APIs that are available in Adobe Commerce (PaaS) and Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service (SaaS).
4: The APIs can be used to perform a wide array of tasks. For example:
5: Create a shopping app. This can be a traditional app that a user downloads on a mobile device. You could also create an app that an employee uses on a showroom floor to help customers make purchases.
6: Integrate with CRM (Customer Relationship Management) or ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) backend systems, such as Salesforce or Xero.
7: Integrate with a CMS (Content Management System). Currently, content tagging is not supported.
8: Adobe Commerce
9: data-src=/_includes/paas-only.md
10: Adobe Commerce on Cloud, Adobe Commerce on-premises, and Magento Open Source all use the same REST API framework. The REST API documentation describes the REST APIs that are available in these versions of Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source.
11: Endpoints
12: Adobe Commerce provides a wide range of REST API endpoints that allow you to perform actions on behalf of Commerce administrators, customers, and guest shoppers. Integrations are also supported.
13: Authentication
14: Adobe Commerce REST APIs support multiple authentication methods, including:
15: Third-party applications authenticate with OAuth 1.0a.
16: Mobile applications authenticate using tokens.
17: Administrators and customers are authenticated with login credentials.
18: URL structure
19: The URL for Adobe Commerce REST endpoints is structured as follows:
20: https://<host>/rest/<store-view-code>/<endpoint>
21: Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service
22: data-src=/_includes/saas-only.md
23: The Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service REST API serves as a critical tool for extending and integrating commerce functionalities, but the endpoints available differ significantly from the REST APIs for Adobe Commerce on Cloud and on-premises deployments.
24: The following key differences are important to consider when planning your REST API integrations with Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service:
25: Endpoints
26: Primarily the Cloud Service REST API differs in that it includes a smaller subset of endpoints. Specifically, the customer and guest REST APIs that are available in Adobe Commerce on Cloud and on-premises deployments are not available in Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service. However, access to similar functionality remains available with the GraphQL APIs.
27: The API reference lists the available endpoints.
28: Authentication
29: In previous versions of Adobe Commerce, you would use authentication tokens to authorize your requests to the REST API. In Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service, you must use Adobe Identity Management Service (IMS) to authenticate your requests.
30: The authentication system supports both interactive user-based workflows and automated server-to-server integrations, ensuring secure and appropriate access for different use cases. Both of these authentication methods require every request to be signed with an IMS Access Token.
31: URL structure
32: In Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service, REST endpoint URLs do not include /rest or the store view code. The store scope is specified via the Store HTTP header.
33: Base format:
34: https://<server>.api.commerce.adobe.com/<tenant-id>/<endpoint>
35: Set the scope with the Store header:
36: Predefined values:
37: Store: all — Execute in the global scope
38: Store: default — Target the default store view (or use your specific store view code)
39: You can also pass any specific store view code: Store: <store_view_code>
40: The following curl command shows the request pattern:
41: curl --location 'https://<server>.api.commerce.adobe.com/<tenant-id>/<endpoint>' \
42: --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
43: --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
44: --header 'Store: <all | default | <store_view_code>>'
45: ....

1: GraphQL overview
2: GraphQL overview
3: GraphQL is a data query language and runtime that revolutionizes how you build and consume APIs. Originally developed by Facebook in 2012 and open-sourced in 2015, GraphQL has become the preferred choice for modern applications that need efficient, flexible, and performant data fetching.
4: Adobe Commerce provides two comprehensive GraphQL implementations that serve as the ideal foundation for building next-generation commerce experiences, including headless storefronts and sophisticated mobile applications.
5: Adobe Commerce on Cloud and on-premises (PaaS) projects can implement the GraphQL schemas that have long been available to Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source projects. Separate schemas are available for core and B2B Commerce functionality and service-based features, including Catalog Service, Live Search, and Recommendations. These schemas do not natively interact, but can be integrated with API Mesh.
6: Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service (SaaS) projects can connect to a supergraph that not only combines and streamlines the schemas available to PaaS projects, but provides instant access to the latest features added in the Storefront Compatability Package and other sources. Therefore, SaaS projects can take advantage of the latest GraphQL features without needing to wait for a new release.
7: data-variant=info
8: data-slots=text
9: If you are migrating from PaaS to SaaS, be aware that the SaaS schema removes all deprecated queries, mutations, and fields, so you can build new applications without worrying about future deprecations. It also replaces the core products and categories queries with their service-based equivalents, also named products and categories. The service-based queries are not backward compatible with the core queries, so you must update your applications to use the new queries. For more information, see Migrate to Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service for general guidelines.
10: Why use GraphQL?
11: Get exactly what you need. Unlike traditional REST APIs that return fixed data structures, GraphQL lets you request exactly the fields you need in a single query. This means faster load times, reduced bandwidth usage, and better user experiences.
12: Superior performance. GraphQL minimizes over-fetching and under-fetching of data, allowing you to optimize performance by fetching only the necessary information in a single request. In addition, minimized data transfer is ideal for mobile and low-bandwidth environments.
13: Enhanced developer experience. GraphQL's strongly typed schema and introspection capabilities provide powerful tools for developers. You can explore the API, get realtime feedback, and leverage auto-completion in modern IDEs, making development faster and more efficient.
14: Getting started with GraphQL
15: Ready to experience the power of Adobe Commerce GraphQL? Here's how to get started:
16: Choose Your GraphQL client. Select a GraphQL IDE or browser extension to explore and test queries and mutations. Some popular options include:
17: GraphiQL
18: Altair GraphQL client
19: Altair Chrome extension
20: Apollo Studio
21: Access your GraphQL endpoint. Your Adobe Commerce GraphQL endpoint is available at:
22: PaaS only https://<commerce-server>/graphql
23: SaaS only https://<region>-<environment>.api.commerce.adobe.com/<tenantId>/graphql
24: Explore the schema. Use the schema browser in your GraphQL IDE or extension to explore the available queries, mutations, and types. This will help you understand the structure of the API and how to construct your requests. You can also use introspection queries to discover the schema programmatically.
25: query IntrospectionQuery {
26: __schema {
27: mutationType {
28: name
29: fields {
30: name
31: description
32: }
33: }
34: queryType {
35: name
36: fields {
37: name
38: description
39: }
40: }
41: }
42: }
43: Run your first query. Try this simple product query to get started:
44: {
45: storeConfig {
46: store_code
47: store_name
48: is_default_store
49: store_group_code
50: is_default_store_group
51: locale
52: base_currency_code
53: default_display_currency_code
54: timezone
55: }
56: }
57: The response will provide you with basic information about your store configuration, such as the store code, name, locale, and currency settings.
58: {
59: data {
60: storeConfig {
61: store_code: "default"
62: store_name: "Default Store View"
63: is_default_store: true
64: store_group_code: "main_website_store"
65: is_default_store_group: true
66: locale: "en_US"
67: base_currency_code: "USD"
68: default_display_currency_code: "USD"
69: timezone: "America/Los_Angeles"
70: }
71: }
72: }
73: Commerce API playground
74: The Commerce API playground enables you to run selected queries against a live instance of Adobe Commerce with Luma sample data. The playground includes example core and Storefront Services queries. You can customize the output of the queries to help you understand the power of our GraphQL APIs.

1: Authentication
2: data-src=/_includes/paas-only.md
3: Authentication
4: data-variant=info
5: data-slots=text
6: This topic is for Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) customers only. Adobe Commerce Cloud Services customers must refer to REST Authentication for details on authentication.
7: For practical implementation guides for Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service (SaaS), see:
8: Create server-to-server integration - Complete guide for automated system integration
9: Generate the IMS access token - User authentication guide
10: Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source allow developers to define web API resources and their permissions in the webapi.xml configuration file. See Services as Web APIs.
11: Before you can make web API calls, you must authenticate your identity and have necessary permissions (authorization) to access the API resource. Authentication allows the application to identify the caller's user type. A user's (administrator, integration, customer, or guest) access rights determine an API call's resource accessibility.
12: Accessible resources
13: The list of resources that you can access depends on your user type. All customers have the same permissions, and as a result the same resources accessible. The preceding statement is true for guest users as well. Each administrator or integration user can have a unique set of permissions which is configured in the Admin. Permissions required to access particular resource are configured in the webapi.xml file. This table lists the resources that each user type can access:
14: User type
15: Accessible resources (defined in webapi.xml)
16: Administrator or Integration
17: Resources for which administrators or integrators are authorized. For example, if administrators are authorized for the Magento_Customer::group resource, they can make a GET /V1/customerGroups/:id call.
18: Customer
19: Resources with anonymous or self permission
20: Guest user
21: Resources with anonymous permission
22: Relationship between acl.xml and webapi.xml
23: The acl.xml file defines the access control list (ACL) for a given module. It defines the available set of permissions to access resources.
24: All acl.xml files across all modules are consolidated to build an ACL tree, which is used to select allowed Admin role resources or third-party integration access (System > Extension > Integration > Add New Integration > Available APIs).
25: Sample customer acl.xml
26: For example, account management, customer configuration, and customer group resource permissions are defined in the Customer module's acl.xml.
27: When a developer creates the Web API configuration file (webapi.xml), the permissions defined in acl.xml are referenced to create access rights for each API resource.
28: Sample (truncated) customer webapi.xml
29: <routes xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
30: xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="urn:magento:module:Magento_Webapi:etc/webapi.xsd">
31: <!-- Customer Group -->
32: <route url="/V1/customerGroups/:id" method="GET">
33: <service class="Magento\Customer\Api\GroupRepositoryInterface" method="getById"/>
34: <resources>
35: <resource ref="Magento_Customer::group"/>
36: </resources>
37: </route>
38: ............
39: .......
40: .....
41: <!-- Customer Account -->
42: <route url="/V1/customers/:customerId" method="GET">
43: <service class="Magento\Customer\Api\CustomerRepositoryInterface" method="getById"/>
44: <resources>
45: <resource ref="Magento_Customer::customer"/>
46: </resources>
47: </route>
48: <route url="/V1/customers" method="POST">
49: <service class="Magento\Customer\Api\AccountManagementInterface" method="createAccount"/>
50: <resources>
51: <resource ref="anonymous"/>
52: </resources>
53: </route>
54: <route url="/V1/customers/:customerId" method="PUT">
55: <service class="Magento\Customer\Api\CustomerRepositoryInterface" method="save"/>
56: <resources>
57: <resource ref="Magento_Customer::manage"/>
58: </resources>
59: </route>
60: <route url="/V1/customers/me" method="PUT">
61: <service class="Magento\Customer\Api\CustomerRepositoryInterface" method="save"/>
62: <resources>
63: <resource ref="self"/>
64: </resources>
65: <data>
66: <parameter name="customer.id" force="true">%customer_id%</parameter>
67: </data>
68: </route>
69: ..........
70: .....
71: ...
72: For example, in the preceding webapi.xml for the customerGroups resource, only a user with Magento_Customer::group authorization can GET /V1/customerGroups/:id. On the other hand, you can create a customer using POST /V1/customers anonymously (or by a guest).
73: Authorization is granted to either an administrator (or an integration) defined in the Admin with the customer group selected as one of the resources in the ACL tree.
74: data-variant=info
75: data-slots=text1, text2
76: A guest or anonymous is a special permission that doesn't need to be defined in acl.xml (and will not show up in the permissions tree in the Admin). It just indicates that the current resource in webapi.xml can be accessed without the need for authentication.
77: Similarly, self is a special access used if you already have an authenticated session with the system. Self access enables a user to access resources they own. For example, GET /V1/customers/me fetches the logged-in customer's details. This is typically useful for JavaScript-based widgets.
78: Web API clients and authentication methods
79: You must use a client, such as a mobile application or an external batch job, to access services using web APIs.
80: Each type of client has a preferred authentication method. To authenticate, use the authentication method for your preferred client:
81: Mobile application authentication
82: Registered users use token-based authentication to make web API calls using a mobile application. The token acts like an electronic key that provides access to the API(s).
83: As a registered account user, you request a token from the Magento token service at the endpoint that is defined for your user type.
84: The token service returns a unique authentication token in exchange for a username and password for an admin or customer account.
85: To prove your identity, specify this token in the Authorization request header on web API calls.
86: Third-party application authentication
87: Third-party applications use OAuth-based authentication to access the web APIs.
88: The third-party Integration registers with Adobe Commerce.
89: Merchants authorize extensions and applications to access or update store data.
90: JavaScript widget authentication (storefront or Admin)
91: Registered users use session-based authentication to log in to the storefront or Admin.
92: A session is identified by a cookie and time out after a period of inactivity. Additionally, you can have a session as a guest user without logging in.
93: As a customer, you log in to the storefront with your customer credentials. As an administrator, you log in to the Admin with your administrator credentials.
94: The web API framework identifies you and controls access to the requested resource.
95: Authentication types
96: The following sections describe tips about which type of authentication method you should use depending on your use case.
97: Token based (Bearer Authentication)
98: This method is a good choice for authenticating customers and Admin users in third-party applications that need to make authorized API calls to the store.
99: Customer Token—Use this token in applications to authorize specific customer and query data related to that customer (for example, customer details, cart, and orders).
100: Admin Token—Use this token in applications to authorize an Admin user and access Admin-related APIs.
101: Request a token and then include it in future requests.
102: data-variant=info
103: data-slots=text
104: You should use this type of authentication mechanism over HTTPS.
105: Integration (Oauth)
106: This method is a good choice for integrating with a third-party system that supports OAuth 1.0a.
107: After activating an integration (self activated), you can use the generated consumer key, consumer secret, access token, and access token secret to provide third-party systems access to Commerce Store resources. You do not need to make calls to the /oauth/token/request or /oauth/token/access endpoints to exchange tokens.
108: If a third-party system provides endpoints, you can use them to activate an integration and link your account. After completing the activation process, a third-party service can use the consumer key, consumer secret, access token, and access token secret provided by Commerce during activation to make API calls.
109: Related topics
110: Proceed to the authentication method for your preferred client:
111: Mobile application. Token-based authentication.
112: Third-party application. OAuth-based authentication.
113: JavaScript widget on the Admin or storefront. Session-based authentication.
114: Extension attribute authentication

26: Authentication and permissions
27: To keep Squarespace merchant site data private and secure,
28: every request to Commerce APIs must be authenticated and have minimum permissions.
29: However, authenticated requests automatically have access to public site data,
30: such as site name, identifier, language, currency, time zone, and location.
31: Read the permission levels for each Commerce API below.
32: Then, depending on your development needs,
33: authenticate requests by using an API key or OAuth access token.
34: Remember: Requests only have access to data for
35: the website that owns the API key or OAuth access token.

38: Read Only: View form submission data; for Zapier integration only
39: Inventory API
40: Read Only: View inventory stock levels
41: Read and Write: Manage inventory stock levels
42: Orders API
43: Read Only: View order, fulfillment, and customer information (name, email, address, and more)
44: Read and Write: View customer information (name, email, address, and more); manage order and fulfillment information
45: Products API
46: Read Only: View product information, including information for any images and variants; view Store Page information
47: Read and Write: Manage product information, including information for any images and variants; view Store Page information
48: Contacts API
49: Read Only: View contact records, address books, and marketing preferences
50: Read and Write: Manage contact records, address books, and marketing preferences
51: Discounts API
52: Read Only: View discount records
53: Read and Write: Manage discount records
54: Webhook Subscriptions API (OAuth only)
55: Read and Write: Create, update, delete, and test webhook subscriptions
56: Profiles API (maintenance mode — new integrations should use the Contacts API)
57: Read Only: View the name, address, email, marketing preferences, and other profile information of customers, subscribers, and other website users
58: Transactions API
59: Read Only: View transactional order, donation data, and customer information (email)
60: Authenticating requests
61: Depending on your development needs,
62: you can use a generated API key or start the OAuth process with Squarespace
63: to become a registered OAuth client. A Squarespace merchant site can use both
64: API keys and OAuth for data access, but Squarespace Extensions are required to use OAuth.
65: Custom applications
66: With Squarespace's Commerce Advanced plan,
67: you can develop a custom application for a Squarespace merchant site.
68: Follow the steps below to generate an API key for a custom application.
69: Log in to a Squarespace site.
70: In the left nav, click Settings; scroll down and click Advanced.
71: Click Developer API Keys.
72: Click the GENERATE KEY button.
73: In the dialog, add a key name under "KEY NAME",
74: and select one or more Commerce APIs under "PERMISSIONS" and permission level.
75: Record the generated key in a safe and secure place.
76: For security reasons, this is the only time the API key is visible.
77: API keys will never expire as long as the merchant site remains active.
78: Commercial development
79: Squarespace Extensions allow customers on any plan
80: to optimize and expand their site in a few clicks.
81: If you'd like to develop a new Extension,
82: start the OAuth client process here.
83: Once you've obtained OAuth credentials, you can use our OAuth 2.0 Guide to learn how to authorize your application to integrate with Squarespace and use Squarespace APIs.
84: Registering an OAuth client, and having it reviewed and approved, only allows OAuth connections with Squarespace.
85: It doesn't list your application in Squarespace Extensions, which is a separate process.

26: Accessing Squarespace APIs using OAuth 2.0
27: Squarespace uses OAuth 2.0 to authorize third-party applications to integrate with Squarespace and consume Squarespace APIs.
28: Terms
29: ClientThird-party application that needs to make Squarespace API calls.
30: User
31: Squarespace customer who wants to integrate their site with a client.
32: Confirmation page
33: Page created by Squarespace for the user to authorize (Allow or Deny) client access to their Squarespace account.
34: Access tokenShort-term token to make authenticated API requests.
35: Refresh tokenLong-term token to obtain new access tokens.
36: Instructions
37: 1. Register the client and obtain OAuth 2.0 credentials
38: Before a client can make Squarespace API calls, the client must be registered with Squarespace as an OAuth client. Start the Oauth client process here.
39: Client name
40: Icon image (.png or .svg format, max size 200kb, 1:1 ratio)
41: Redirect URI(s) - For example, https://thirdpartyapp.com/oauth/connect
42: Initiate URL* - For example, https://thirdpartyapp.com/oauth/initiate.
43: Link to Client's Terms and Conditions
44: Link to Client's Privacy Policy
45: *Applies only to Squarespace partner apps. These will be linked from inside Squarespace.
46: We will review your registration and respond with your_client_id and your_client_secret as soon as possible. These credentials are used in the subsequent steps.
47: Note: This review only approves your client for OAuth connections with Squarespace. It doesn't add your application to Squarespace Extensions. Listing there is a separate process.
48: 2. Prompt the user to authorize client access
49: The /authorize URL prompts the user to authorize client access to their Squarespace data and serves as the confirmation page. If a user selects Allow, OAuth 2.0 authentication is started between the client and Squarespace APIs. Append required and any optional parameters to the GET /authorize endpoint; all parameter values should be URL-encoded.
50: Code
51: GET https://login.squarespace.com/api/1/login/oauth/provider/authorize
52: Query parameterRequirementValue
53: client_idRequired
54: Alphanumeric value for your_client_id that was supplied by
55: Squarespace in Step 1.
56: redirect_uriRequiredString; the full redirect URI sent to Squarespace in Step 1.
57: scopeRequired
58: String; comma-separated list of client permission values (see below)
59: for API access. The confirmation page always displays website(s) for
60: user selection for scope=website.*
61: website.orders
62: Send order data and mark orders as fulfilled.
63: website.orders.read
64: View order and fulfillment information.
65: website.transactions.read
66: Access transactional order and donation data.
67: website.inventory
68: View and update inventory stock levels.
69: website.inventory.read
70: View inventory stock levels.
71: website.products
72: View product information and modify products.
73: website.products.read
74: View product information.
75: website.contacts
76: View customer contact information and address book entries; create, update, and delete contacts and address book entries.
77: website.contacts.read
78: View customer contact information and address book entries.
79: website.discounts
80: View and manage discounts.
81: website.discounts.read
82: View discounts.
83: Example:
84: &scope=website.inventory,website.orders
85: stateRequired
86: Alphanumeric random value generated by client. You'll use it in
87: Step 3, Implement redirect URI, to prevent CSRF attacks.
88: website_idConditionally Required
89: Alphanumeric value for a Squarespace site ID.
90: When a logged-in user initiates an OAuth connection from Squarespace, this
91: value is appended as a query parameter on the provided initiate URL. Partners must
92: pass this parameter back to the GET /authorize endpoint.
93: If an OAuth connection is initiated by a logged-out user, Squarespace will not
94: include a website_id parameter on the initiate URL. Partners should not pass any
95: website_id parameter back to the GET /authorize
96: endpoint in these cases. Instead, the user will be prompted to select a website
97: on the confirmation page.
98: access_typeOptional
99: String; use offline for long-term API access. For more
100: information, see Token expiration and long-term access. Omit
101: parameter for short-term API access.
102: Authorize URL example with parameters
103: Note: Parameter values are in plain text and not URL-encoded for example purposes.
104: Code
105: https://login.squarespace.com/api/1/login/oauth/provider/authorize?client_id=fGBjMDBaUHli&redirect_uri=http://localhost:8090/oauth/callback&scope=website.inventory,website.orders&state=2BsmGS9AAzFppUmcoIagOLj4iKII
106: 3. Implement redirect URI
107: Both Allow or Deny on the confirmation page directs the user to the client redirect URI (i.e., the redirect_uri specified in Step 2) with query parameters appended by Squarespace. For Allow, the redirect URI should verify the state parameter and match it against state value that was appended for the /authorize endpoint. This verification prevents CSRF attacks. Squarespace doesn't provide guidelines for Deny implementation.
108: ParameterValue
109: error
110: String; access_denied if user selects Deny
111: on confirmation page. Parameter isn't appended if user selects
112: Allow.
113: state
114: Alphanumeric value; not present if user selects Deny.
115: code
116: Alphanumeric value used in step 4. Request access token. Value is
117: initially URL-encoded and should be decoded prior to sending in the
118: access token request. Valid for two minutes and only for one-time use.
119: Not present if user selects Deny.
120: 4. Request access token
121: Code
122: POST https://login.squarespace.com/api/1/login/oauth/provider/tokens
123: The client makes a POST /tokens call with required and any optional parameters for an access token from Squarespace. Access tokens in the response are only valid for 30 minutes. For more information, see Token expiration and long-term access.
124: Parameters
125: BodyRequirementValue
126: grant_typeOptional
127: String; default is authorization_code; use authorization_code for
128: your first request. For long-term API access, use refresh_token for
129: all subsequent requests.
130: code
131: Required if grant_type=authorization_code
132: Alphanumeric value of code passed to redirect URI.
133: redirect_uri
134: Required if grant_type=authorization_code
135: String; redirect_uri used for the /authorize endpoint.
136: refresh_token
137: Required if grant_type=refresh_token
138: String; use application/json or application/x-www-form-urlencoded
139: Header
140: AuthorizationRequired
141: Follow the steps below to build the header value:
142: Use your Squarespace OAuth 2.0 credentials to construct a string in
143: the format: your_client_id:your_client_secret
144: Encode the string from Step 1 into base-64
145: Add Basic<space> as a prefix to the encoded string from Step 2
146: Example
147: your_client_id: abc123
148: your_client_secret: 12secret345
149: Authorization after base-64
150: Basic YWJjMTIzOjEyc2VjcmV0MzQ1
151: Content-TypeRequiredString; use application/json or application/x-www-form-urlencoded
152: User-AgentRequired
153: String; If you see an error referencing SEC-43, a User-Agent header is
154: missing
155: Example Response
156: JavascriptCode
157: {
158: "token_type": "bearer",
159: "access_token": "T1|Rr0Wc95uu3cSeBh06yB...",
160: // expires 30 minutes after it's created ...
161: "access_token_expires_at": "1553532363.542",
162: }
163: 5. Make API requests
164: After you obtain an access token, you can make API requests.
165: Endpoint:
166: https://api.squarespace.com/...
167: Authorization format:
168: Bearer<space><access-token-from-tokens-response>
169: Using the sample response from Step 4, Authorization would have the value:
170: Bearer T1|Rr0Wc95uu3cSeBh06yB...
171: Token expiration and long-term access
172: When a response from POST /tokens is received, access_token is only valid for 30 minutes. For long-term Squarespace API access, the client has to prompt the user to reauthorize using the GET /authorize endpoint or use refresh tokens.
173: Refresh tokens
174: To get a refresh token, add access_type=offline as a parameter to the GET /authorize request. When the client makes a POST /tokens call, the response includes refresh_token. Use the refresh token to get new tokens by making another POST /tokens call with the parameters below. The refresh token expires after seven days.
175: grant_type=refresh_token
176: refresh_token=<previous-refresh-token-value>
177: Note: Each POST /tokens call with a refresh_token parameter results in a new refresh_token and access_token. Refresh tokens are effectively one-time use—the original refresh token is invalidated as soon as the new access token is used. If long-term API access is required, the client should replace the stored refresh token with the most recent refresh_token. Note that obtaining new tokens doesn't revoke existing access tokens.
178: Sample response from /tokens:
179: Code
180: {
181: "token": "T1|Rr0Wc95uu3cSeBh06yB...",
182: "token_type": "bearer",
183: // expires 30 mins after creation
184: "access_token": "T1|Rr0Wc95uu3cSeBh06yB...",
185: "access_token_expires_at": "1553532363.542",
186: // expires 7 days after creation
187: "refresh_token": "1|KYUYh35zcwzx4Zt/oty3...",
188: "refresh_token_expires_at": "1554135363.542"
189: }
190: Sample use case with refresh tokens
191: Client has to poll orders from a user site indefinitely and needs to call the Squarespace API once
192: per minute.
193: User authorizes client access to Squarespace APIs via confirmation page; client makes a POST /tokens call and obtains access and refresh tokens in response.
194: Client secures and stores the values below for current record (CR):
195: access_token=<at-1>
196: access_token_expires_at=<timestamp>
197: refresh_token=<rt-1>
198: Prior to each API call, client checks if:
199: CR.access_token_expires_at - currentTime > 10 seconds
200: If true, client makes an API call with CR.access_token.
201: If false, client makes a POST /tokens call with refresh_token=CR.refresh_token as a parameter for new access and refreshntokens; client stores new token values in CR:
202: access_token=<at-2>
203: access_token_expires_at=<timestamp>
204: refresh_token=<rt-2>
205: Client repeats Steps 2 and 3 indefinitely.
206: Invalid tokens and revoking access
207: Tokens become invalid in two ways: the tokens expire or the user revokes client access from the Squarespace UI. In either case, the user has to reauthorize client access to get new access tokens.
208: When an access token is invalid, Squarespace responds to API requests with 401 Unauthorized. If a client receives a 401, they should notify the user that their Squarespace integration requires reauthorization.

46: Ecwid REST API allows you to access and manage any store data, payment and shipping methods, and storefront settings.
47: We use OAuth 2.0 authorization simplified for single-store customizations, JSON-formatted data, and a clear structure.
48: Please note that our REST API has rate limits.
49: We accept up to 600 requests per minute per token. If you exceed the limit, all subsequent requests will be ignored with an error 429 and a "Retry-After": N header (number N is a cooldown) . If more requests continue to come from a non-working token, Ecwid will block it for much longer after 20 requests per minute or a total of 600 requests with non-working tokens per IP.
50: Ecwid API also supports gzip encoding through the "Accept-Encoding": "gzip" header.

26: Frequently asked questions
27: What can I sell on Gumroad?
28: Digital products, e-books, courses, tutorials, and memberships—almost anything! Creators in just about every industry use (and love) Gumroad, from digital artists, writers, musicians and other creative-types to business-minded entrepreneurs and tech gurus like our SaaS creators. A better question is, "What can't I sell on Gumroad?"
29: What can't I sell on Gumroad?
30: Outside of physical goods, things like illegal or illicit goods or services, securities & financial instruments, credit repair, gambling & lotteries, harassment & extremist content, copyright infringement & piracy, or obscene or adult content are not permitted on Gumroad. A full list can be found here.
31: How do I get paid?
32: Gumroad's goal is to help creators make a living doing what they love, so we make it as simple as possible to get paid. How we pay creators, whether through direct deposit or PayPal, varies by country.
33: What are the fees?
34: Unlike other platforms, Gumroad doesn't charge you a monthly fee. Instead, our fees are deducted as a small percentage of every sale, so we only make money when you do.
35: Can I use Gumroad for memberships?
36: Yes!
37: Whether it's for a podcast, online course, or SaaS subscriptions, Gumroad makes it easy to manage memberships.
38: How does Gumroad handle taxes?
39: Gumroad is your merchant of record, which means we automatically handle all sales tax collection and remittance worldwide. You don't need to manage any tax settings or applications - we take care of everything.
40: What do I need to do about taxes?
41: Nothing! The change took effect on January 1, 2025, and our Terms of Service reflect it. You can continue selling as usual.
42: What about international sales?
43: We'll handle all tax obligations for your global sales automatically. You don't need to worry about VAT, GST, or any other international tax requirements.
44: What happens to my tax collection settings?
45: All tax settings will be automatically disabled in your dashboard. This includes both the state tax settings in your creator profile and any product-specific tax settings. You won't need to manage these anymore since we'll handle all tax collection automatically.
46: Will Gumroad collect taxes everywhere?
47: We collect taxes in regions where we have tax obligations as a merchant of record. This varies by location, and we automatically handle the appropriate tax collection for each sale.
48: Need a Reseller Certificate from Gumroad?
49: Some creators may have an obligation to file sales tax (or other indirect tax) returns already, and will need to report their sales on Gumroad as "sales to other retailers for purposes of resale", which are not taxable. To justify this treatment to your tax authority, you will need to download and save this Reseller Certificate.

299: We use Docker to setup the services for development environment.
300: For MacOS: Download the Docker app from the Docker website
301: For Linux:
302: sudo wget -qO- https://get.docker.com/ | sh
303: sudo usermod -aG docker $(whoami)
304: MySQL & Percona Toolkit
305: Install a local version of MySQL 8.4.x to match the version running in production.
306: The local version of MySQL is a dependency of the Ruby mysql2 gem. You do not need to start an instance of the MySQL service locally. The app will connect to a MySQL instance running in the Docker container.
307: For MacOS:
308: brew install mysql@8.4 percona-toolkit
309: brew link --force mysql@8.4
310: # to use Homebrew's `openssl`:
311: brew install openssl
312: bundle config --global build.mysql2 --with-opt-dir="$(brew --prefix openssl)"
313: # ensure MySQL is not running as a service
314: brew services stop mysql@8.4
315: For Linux:
316: MySQL:
317: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/linux-installation.html
318: apt install libmysqlclient-dev
319: Percona Toolkit: https://www.percona.com/doc/percona-toolkit/LATEST/installation.html
320: ImageMagick
321: We use imagemagick for preview editing.
322: For MacOS: brew install imagemagick
323: For Linux: sudo apt-get install imagemagick
324: FFmpeg
325: We use ffprobe that comes with FFmpeg package to fetch metadata from video files.
326: For MacOS: brew install ffmpeg
327: For Linux: sudo apt-get install ffmpeg
328: PDFtk
329: We use pdftk to stamp PDF files with the Gumroad logo and the buyers' emails.
330: For MacOS: Download from here
331: Note: pdftk may be blocked by Apple's firewall. If this happens, go to Settings > Privacy & Security and click "Open Anyways" to allow the installation.
332: For Linux: sudo apt-get install pdftk
333: wkhtmltopdf
334: While generating invoices, to convert HTML to PDF, PDFKit expects wkhtmltopdf to be installed on your system. Download and install the version 0.12.6 for your platform.
335: Note similar to pdftk, this may also be blocked by Apple's firewall on MacOS. Follow a similar process as above.
336: Installation
337: Bundler and gems
338: We use Bundler to install Ruby gems.
339: gem install bundler
340: Install gems:
341: bundle install
342: Also make sure to install dotenv as it is required for some console commands:
343: gem install dotenv
344: npm and Node.js dependencies
345: Make sure the correct version of npm is enabled:
346: corepack enable
347: Install dependencies:
348: npm install
349: Configuration
350: Set up Custom credentials
351: App can be booted without any custom credentials. But if you would like to use services that require custom credentials (e.g. S3, Stripe, Resend, etc.), you can copy the .env.example file to .env and fill in the values.
352: Running Locally
353: Start Docker services
354: If you installed Docker Desktop (on a Mac or Windows machine), you can run the following command to start the Docker services:
355: make local
356: If you are on Linux, or installed Docker via a package manager on a mac, you may need superuser access to expose container ports. To do that, use sudo make local instead.
357: This command will not terminate. You run this in one tab and start the application in another tab.
358: If you want to run Docker services in the background, use LOCAL_DETACHED=true make local instead.
359: Set up the database
360: bin/rails db:prepare
361: For Linux (Debian / Ubuntu) you might need the following:
362: apt install libxslt-dev libxml2-dev
363: Start the application
364: bin/dev
365: This starts the Rails server, the JavaScript build system, and a Sidekiq worker.
366: You can now access the application at http://localhost:3000. Seller subdomains and the asset/api hosts use *.localhost (e.g. http://seller.localhost:3000, http://api.localhost:3000) — modern browsers auto-resolve these to 127.0.0.1, so no /etc/hosts edits are needed.
367: Local dev limitations
368: *.localhost over HTTP is treated as a secure context by browsers (so Stripe.js, Stripe Elements, and other secure-context APIs work), but a couple of features that need either HTTPS or a registrable cookie domain don't work in this setup:
369: Apple Pay — Stripe requires HTTPS for Apple Pay domain registration. Workaround: expose the app over HTTPS with ngrok (ngrok http 3000) and register the resulting hostname in the Stripe Apple Pay dashboard.
370: Cross-subdomain cookies (affiliate attribution, _gumroad_guid, multi-account "switch seller", session) — browsers reject Domain=localhost, so cookies set on localhost:3000 aren't sent to seller.localhost:3000. Test these flows on a single host, or front the app with a local HTTPS reverse proxy on a registrable hostname (e.g. gumroad.test via mkcert) where Domain=.gumroad.test works.
371: Testing
372: Run the full test suite:
373: bin/rspec
374: Run a single file or specific test:
375: bin/rspec spec/requests/dashboard_spec.rb
376: bin/rspec spec/requests/dashboard_spec.rb:75
377: Dependencies
378: Before running tests:
379: make local # start Docker services (db, Redis, etc.)
380: RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails db:setup # set up the test database
381: RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails js:export # generate JS constants for the test environment
382: Integration tests
383: Integration specs use Capybara with Selenium driving Chrome. Install Chrome from google.com/chrome.
384: See docs/testing.md for details on preventing flaky specs, VCR cassettes, debugging widgets, and purchase testing with Stripe/PayPal.
385: Development
386: Logging in
387: You can log in with the username seller@gumroad.com and the password password. The two-factor authentication code is 000000.
388: Read more about logging in as a user with a different team role at Users & authentication.
389: Resetting Elasticsearch indices
390: You will need to explicitly reindex Elasticsearch to populate the indices after setup, otherwise you will see index_not_found_exception errors when you visit the dev application. You can reset them using:
391: # Run this in a rails console:
392: DevTools.delete_all_indices_and_reindex_all
393: Push Notifications
394: To send push notifications:
395: INITIALIZE_RPUSH_APPS=true bundle exec rpush start -e development -f
396: Common Development Tasks
397: Rails console:
398: bin/rails c
399: Rake tasks:
400: bin/rake task_name
401: Linting
402: We use ESLint for JS, and Rubocop for Ruby. Your editor should support displaying and fixing issues reported by these inline, and CI checks these on every push.
403: If you'd like, you can run git config --local core.hooksPath .githooks to check for these locally when committing.
404: Common Issues
405: macOS Error When Running Tests (Related to fork())
406: objc[11912]: +[__NSCFConstantString initialize] may have been in progress in another thread when fork() was called.
407: objc[11912]: +[__NSCFConstantString initialize] may have been in progress in another thread when fork() was called. We cannot safely call it or ignore it in the fork() child process. Crashing instead. Set a breakpoint on objc_initializeAfterForkError to debug.
408: This issue occurs on macOS due to how the fork() system call interacts with multithreaded Objective-C applications—commonly triggered when Spring is enabled during testing.
409: How to Fix:
410: Temporarily disable Spring before running your tests to avoid this error.
411: export DISABLE_SPRING=1
412: bin/rspec spec/requests/balance_pages_spec.rb
413: This will disable Spring for the current session, allowing the tests to run without triggering the fork()-related crash.

600: What is the Selling Partner API?
601: This topic describes the REST-based Selling Partner API.
602: The Selling Partner API (SP-API) is a REST-based API that helps sellers and vendors access their data on orders, shipments, payments, inventory, and other business information. The API supports building applications that automate Amazon business operations.
603: Key features
604: With SP-API, developers can create applications that help sellers and vendors:
605: Process orders automatically, send instant shipping confirmations, and update tracking information in real-time.
606: Access real-time order status, inventory levels across warehouses, and payment reports.
607: Set up automated workflows to create a new listing, sync inventory across multiple Amazon stores, update pricing based on market conditions, and manage fulfillment operations.
608: Subscribe to notifications to receive alerts when orders are placed, updates about shipping status changes, and updates about traffic metrics for products listed on Amazon.
609: Automate the retrieval of financial transactions, tax information, and invoices.
610: Global application registration and secure authorization
611: With SP-API, developers register once in their preferred region and Amazon store. After registering, selling partners can initiate an OAuth authorization workflow from the Selling Partner Appstore detail page or from a developer website from any region or Amazon store. OAuth authorization provides secure access to data with permissions.
612: Developer tools
613: SP-API includes:
614: Tools to generate SDKs that provide access to all SP-API endpoints with built-in LWA token exchange and authentication.
615: A sandbox environment for select SP-APIs to test applications before production deployment.
616: A Data Kiosk API to obtain seller sales and traffic data. A Data Kiosk Schema Explorer is also available to help build custom queries for the Data Kiosk API.
617: Get started with SP-API
618: To get started with SP-API, refer to Onboarding to the SP-API.

600: Selling Partner API Sandbox
601: Use the SP-API sandbox to make test calls.
602: The Selling Partner API (SP-API) provides two hosted and one local sandbox environment that you can use to test your applications without affecting production data or triggering real-world events. The SP-API static sandbox uses pattern matching to return static, mock responses. The SP-API dynamic sandbox routes requests to a sandbox backend that returns realistic responses based on the request parameters. The Sample AI Sandbox is a locally deployed sandbox that uses AI to generate dynamic responses based on your requests.
603: 🚧
604: Important
605: Use the hosted sandbox environments to test functionality, not scalability. Calls to sandbox endpoints are subject to these throttling limits: rate = five requests per second; burst = 15. For more information about throttling, refer to Usage Plans and Rate Limits in the Selling Partner API.
606: If you use a hosted SP-API sandbox environment to test a call that requires a Restricted Data Token (RDT), you must get the RDT from the production environment and pass it to your sandbox call. For information about RDT, refer to the Tokens API Use Case Guide.
