680: SP-API static sandbox
681: Making static sandbox calls is identical to making production calls, except you direct calls to the Selling Partner API sandbox endpoints. Calling the sandbox endpoints returns static, mock responses for all SP-APIs. You can refer to these mock responses in the Swagger model JSON file for the API that you want to call. For more information, refer to Make a static sandbox call.
682: The SP-API static sandbox works like many mock-based frameworks. It uses pattern matching to return a specified response when the specified parameters are present. When a developer sends a request that includes the specified parameters, they receive a response defined in one of the following objects:
683: Static sandbox JSON objects
684: JSON
685: "x-amzn-api-sandbox":
686: {
687: "static": [
688: {
689: "request":
690: {
691: "parameters":
692: {
693: …
694: }
695: },
696: "response":
697: {
698: …
699: }
700: }
701: ]
702: }
703: While these objects contain the parameters needed to match a mock response, they don't necessarily contain all parameters required for a successful response. To get a successful response, be sure that your request is valid and includes all required parameters as defined in the corresponding Swagger model.
704: To make a static sandbox call, use the following procedure:
705: Step 1. Check the JSON model for request parameters
706: Open the JSON model for your API from the Sandbox support by API table.
707: Search the JSON for an x-amzn-api-sandbox object that contains a "static" array.
708: The static sandbox JSON objects contain request and response examples for static sandbox calls to the API operation in which they appear. If the request example contains parameters, use them in the following step.
709: Step 2. Make a static sandbox call to an API
710: Make a static sandbox call to an API in the same way you would make a production call, with these differences:
711: Include the parameters from Step 1. Check the JSON model for request parameters in your call. If the API requires parameters in addition to those, be sure to also include those required parameters in your call.
712: Direct your call to one of the Selling Partner API sandbox endpoints.
713: You should receive a response that matches the payload object contained in the static sandbox JSON object from Step 1.
714: SP-API dynamic sandbox
715: Making dynamic sandbox calls is identical to making production calls, except you direct calls to Selling Partner API sandbox endpoints. The dynamic sandbox proxies (forwards) calls to a sandbox backend, which returns an appropriate response given the request parameters. Because you are not limited to exact pattern matching, you can make requests and receive responses that are potentially stateful and react to input. For example, you might want to verify the shipping charges for different ship-to addresses. The sandbox backend capabilities for that API section determine what you can do.
716: To determine which operations support dynamic sandbox calls, review the Swagger model JSON for your API. An operation supports calls to the dynamic sandbox if the operation includes the following object:
717: JSON
718: "x-amzn-api-sandbox":
719: {
720: "dynamic": {}
721: }
722: The object can be found at either the operation or path level. When at the path level, all operations within the path can make calls to the dynamic sandbox.
723: To make a dynamic sandbox call, use the following procedure:
724: Step 1. Check the JSON model for operations that support dynamic sandbox calls
725: Open the JSON model for your API from the Sandbox support by API table. APIs marked "Dynamic" in the table support dynamic sandbox calls.
726: To confirm at the operation level, search the JSON for:
727: JSON
728: "x-amzn-api-sandbox":
729: {
730: "dynamic": {}
731: }
732: If the operation contains this object at the path or operation level, the dynamic sandbox is supported for that operation.
733: Step 2. Make a dynamic sandbox call to an API
734: Make a dynamic sandbox call to an API in the same way you would make a production call, except direct your call to one of the Selling Partner API sandbox endpoints.
735: Sample AI sandbox for SP-API
736: The sample AI sandbox for SP-API is a local development tool for testing SP-API integrations before deploying to production. It validates requests against SP-API OpenAPI schemas, simulates API responses using an AI agent backed by Amazon Bedrock, and allows dynamic test data generation based on your test scenario.
737: To make an AI sandbox call, use the following procedure:
738: Step 1. Check prerequisites
739: Node.js 22+ (the project extends @tsconfig/node22)
740: npm (ships with Node.js)
741: AWS credentials configured in your environment with access to Amazon Bedrock (the app uses Claude Haiku via @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime)
742: Step 2. Download the application
743: Download the application from GitHub.
744: Step 3. Install and run
745: Run the following commands:
746: Bash
747: npm install
748: npm run build
749: npm run start
750: The server starts on http://localhost:9001 by default.
751: Report feedback and issues
752: You can report issues on GitHub.
753: Sandbox-only operations
754: The sandbox environments support optional APIs that are sandbox-only and can succeed only when directed to one of the Selling Partner API sandbox endpoints. To determine which operations are sandbox-only, review the Swagger model JSON for the API section. An operation that is sandbox-only contains "x-amzn-api-sandbox-only": true at either the operation or path level. When at the path level, all operations within the path are sandbox-only.
755: Sandbox-only operations supplement the production API so that you can create test workflows that are not possible using the production API operations. For example, you might have a use case where a data item is instantiated through the user interface, but not through an API. For testing purposes, a sandbox-only API can create the data item, which enables more complete test workflows.
756: SP-API sandbox endpoints
757: The SP-API has sandbox endpoints for the North America, Europe, and Far East selling regions. These endpoints apply to the hosted static and dynamic sandboxes only. The sample AI sandbox runs locally on http://localhost:9001.
758: Selling regionEndpointAWS Region
759: North America (Canada, US, Mexico, and Amazon Brazil stores)https://sandbox.sellingpartnerapi-na.amazon.comus-east-1
760: Europe (Spain, UK, France, Netherlands, Germany, Italy, Sweden, Poland, Egypt, Turkey, United Arab Emirates, and Amazon India stores)https://sandbox.sellingpartnerapi-eu.amazon.comeu-west-1
761: Far East (Singapore, Australia, and Amazon Japan stores)https://sandbox.sellingpartnerapi-fe.amazon.comus-west-2

153: Amazon Selling Partner
154: Skills for managing an Amazon seller account via SP-API, through the Amazon Selling Partner Connector (MCP). Write actions are always human-in-the-loop (drafted for your approval).
155: Connector
156: The bundled .mcp.json registers the Amazon Selling Partner Connector (MCP server) at
157: https://sellingpartner-ai.amazon.com/mcp. You authorize
158: access through the standard Seller Central OAuth consent flow; the assistant can only use
159: tools allowed by your Seller Central roles. Write actions are drafted for your approval.
160: Skills
161: seller-analytics — seller performance metrics (inventory, traffic, sales); discovers metric IDs before querying.
162: finance-month-end-closer — close and reconcile a completed Amazon month: reconcile net proceeds against settlements, confirm payout statuses, help match bank deposits (seller-supplied; no bank integration), and produce an accountant-ready summary. Read-and-explain only; never files, submits, pays, or moves money.
163: stockout-prevention — quantify stockout risk from days-of-supply and velocity, recommend how much to reorder and by when, and check the inbound-shipment gap. Gives no pricing advice in either direction; if you name a specific price it will draft that exact change for your approval.
164: fba-inbound-management — full FBA inbound plan workflow (create -> packing -> placement -> transportation -> confirm) with approval gates.
165: listing-troubleshooter — the router for "something's wrong with my listing"; scans status/issues and routes to the right specialist.
166: listing-issues — diagnose and fix reported listing issues (suppressions, attribute errors) with preview -> approve.
167: listing-buyability — why a listing isn't buyable (offer, completeness, inventory) and fix the offer with approval.
168: listing-searchability — why a listing isn't found + search-content optimization with approval.
169: listing-compliance — a pre-flight compliance gate run before any compliance-sensitive listing write (claims, ingredients, category, condition, images, identifiers); advisory, never writes.
170: invite-secondary-users — guide the account admin to grant AI-agent access to secondary users via Seller Central Manage Agents (advisory; UI action).
171: support-case-helper — route the seller to Amazon Seller Support and prepare a clean, PII-free case summary; never submits without explicit confirmation.
172: sp-api-knowledge — answer SP-API developer questions and guide integration design, grounded in the SP-API documentation.
173: Commands
174: /sp-stockout-check — run the stockout-prevention workflow.
175: /sp-fix-listing — find and fix suppressed/inactive listings.
176: /sp-sales-drop — diagnose why sales dropped and get safe next steps.
177: Data sent
178: When you use these skills, the assistant sends requests to the Amazon Selling Partner Connector (MCP) at (https://sellingpartner-ai.amazon.com/mcp) over an authenticated connection:
179: What is sent: the tool calls the skills make on your behalf (e.g. requests for your
180: inventory, sales/traffic analytics, listing status, or a drafted listing/price change) and
181: the parameters those calls need (such as your Merchant Token / marketplace and the SKU/ASIN
182: in question). Your prompt text is processed by your AI assistant per its own terms.
183: What comes back: your Amazon business data (inventory, analytics, listing details) that
184: the gateway returns for the calls you approved.
185: Authorization & scope: access is granted through the Seller Central OAuth consent flow
186: and is limited to the tools your Seller Central roles allow. Write actions are never executed
187: without your explicit approval.
188: Not sent by these skills: the skills do not transmit data to any non-Amazon endpoint,
189: and do not persist your account identifiers or data beyond the session. Some skills
190: (e.g. support-case-helper) explicitly redact PII from any summary they produce.
191: Privacy: data handled by Amazon is subject to the
192: Amazon.com Privacy Notice.
193: Data processed by your AI assistant is subject to that assistant's own terms and privacy policy.

208: commerce-sdk
209: The Salesforce Commerce SDK allows easy interaction with the Salesforce B2C Commerce platform APIs on the Node.js runtime. For a more lightweight SDK, which works in a browser and Node.js for the shopper experience, see our Isomorphic SDK
210: Visit the Commerce Cloud Developer Center to learn more about Salesforce Commerce. The developer center has API documentation, getting started guides, community forums, and more.
211: ​
212: Documentation
213: An auto-generated documentation site provides comprehensive reference for all available endpoints and types across API classes. Following the v5.0.0 release, the underlying SDK file structure has been reorganized, introducing additional layers of imports/exports that may affect navigation.
214: Navigating the Documentation
215: For API Classes:
216: Accessing API Classes: Click on the API class name (e.g., shopperProducts) on the right hand side
217: Viewing Endpoints: Scroll to the Classes section and click the corresponding API class link (e.g., ShopperProducts) to see available endpoints and their parameters
218: Type Definitions: Scroll to the Type aliases section for available types
219: Navigating Back to API Classes: To return to the main documentation page with all API classes listed on the right sidebar, click on Globals in the navigation.
220: Utility Classes: Utility classes and methods such as clientConfig and helpers maintain the same structure as previous versions.
221: NOTES:
222: Type Access: API class types are accessible through the <api_class>Types namespace (e.g., ShopperProductsTypes). Individual types can be accessed as ShopperProductsTypes.Product.
223: Type References: The References section under API classes in the generated documentation may show duplicate entries. This occurs because types are exported both at their original definition and under the API class namespace. Both references point to the same underlying type definition.
224: V4 Migration Guide: Starting in v5, API classes will no longer be exported under API family namespaces. See the Sample Code section for migration examples.
225: Supporting Files: The SDK includes additional supporting modules beyond the helpers SLAS functions. The types module provides common type definitions shared across API classes, while the version module automatically implements user agent headers for all requests. The user agent value follows the format commerce-sdk@<version> based on the current SDK version.
226: ⚠️ Planned API Changes ⚠️
227: Shopper Context
228: Starting July 31st 2024, all endpoints in the Shopper context API will require the siteId parameter for new customers. This field is marked as optional for backward compatibility and will be changed to mandatory tentatively by January 2025. You can read more about the planned change here in the notes section.
229: Shopper Login (SLAS)
230: SLAS will soon require new tenants to pass channel_id as an argument for retrieving guest access tokens. You can read more about the planned change here.
231: Please be aware that existing tenants are on a temporary allow list and will see no immediate disruption to service. We do ask that all users seek to adhere to the channel_id requirement before the end of August to enhance your security posture before the holiday peak season.
232: In practice, we recommend that customers using the SLAS helper functions upgrade to v4.0.0 of the commerce-sdk.
233: ⚠️ Planned SDK Changes ⚠️
234: Encoding path parameters
235: In the next major version release, the SDK will encode special characters (UTF-8 based on SCAPI guidelines) in path parameters by default. Please see the Encoding special characters section for more details.
236: Prerequisites
237: Download and install Node.js and npm here.
238: ​
239: Note: Requirements: Node ^20.x or ^22.x. To use a different version of Node.js for other projects, you can manage multiple versions of Node.js with nvm. ​
240: Node.js version compatibility
241: A regression in Node.js 24.17.0 and 22.23.0 caused libraries built on node-fetch@2 to throw false ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE ("Premature close") errors when reusing keep-alive connections. The security fix in those releases added a listener to the socket 'data' event, which node-fetch@2 misreads as a truncated response (nodejs/node#63989).
242: Note: commerce-sdk is not affected by this regression. Its HTTP layer is built on make-fetch-happen, which does not use the socket-listener heuristic that triggers the false error. The companion Isomorphic SDK does depend on node-fetch@2 directly on its Node.js path, so it is affected; the upgrade guidance below applies to it as to any node-fetch@2 consumer.
243: If your application or another dependency uses node-fetch@2, upgrade to a Node.js release that contains the upstream fix: on the 24.x line use 24.18.0 or later (avoid 24.17.0); on the 22.x line use 22.23.1 or later (avoid 22.23.0). The fixed releases retain the security patch that the regression rode in on, so upgrade forward rather than downgrading.
244: Newer "Current"-line releases (Node 26.x) that shipped the same security patch are affected as well. As of June 24, 2026 no fixed 26.x release had shipped; check the Node 26.x changelog for a release that contains the upstream fix. For production, prefer an LTS line (24.x or 22.x) on the fixed versions above.
245: Installation
246: Use npm to install the Commerce SDK.
247: ​
248: npm install commerce-sdk
249: Usage
250: To use an SDK client, instantiate an object of that client and configure these parameters.
251: Note: These are optional parameters.
252: Parameter
253: Description
254: baseUri
255: URL of the service with which the SDK interacts. If the baseUri isn't provided, the default baseUri for the relevant RAML file is used.
256: clientId
257: ID of the client account created with Salesforce Commerce.
258: organizationId
259: The unique identifier for your Salesforce identity.
260: shortCode
261: Region specific merchant ID.
262: siteId
263: A unique site ID (for example, RefArch or SiteGenesis).
264: Sample Code
265: /**
266: * Sample TypeScript code that shows how Commerce SDK can access Salesforce Commerce
267: * APIs.
268: *
269: * For more information, see [Get started with Salesforce Commerce B2C APIs](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/commerce-api/guide/get-started.html).
270: */
271: // Import the SDK in TypeScript
272: // tsc requires the --esModuleInterop flag for this
273: // Starting in v5, API classes will no longer be namespaced under API family
274: import { ShopperSearch, ShopperLogin, helpers, slasHelpers } from "commerce-sdk";
275: // For v4 and below, you'll have to import the API family first
276: // import { Search, Customer, helpers, slasHelpers } from "commerce-sdk";
277: // const loginClient = new Customer.ShopperLogin(config);
278: // const searchClient = new Search.ShopperSearch(config);
279: // Older Node.js versions can instead use:
280: // const { ClientConfig, helpers, slasHelpers Search } = require("commerce-sdk");
281: // Types for each individual API can be imported as <api_name>Types starting in v5
282: import type { ShopperLoginTypes } from "commerce-sdk"
283: // demo client credentials, if you have access to your own please replace them below.
284: // do not store client secret as plaintext. Store it in a secure location.
285: // For guidance on generating a private client with a client secret, please refer to:
286: // https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/pwa-kit-managed-runtime/guide/use-a-slas-private-client.html
287: const CLIENT_SECRET = "<INSERT_CLIENT_SECRET>";
288: const CLIENT_ID = "da422690-7800-41d1-8ee4-3ce983961078";
289: const ORG_ID = "f_ecom_zzte_053";
290: const SHORT_CODE = "kv7kzm78";
291: const SITE_ID = "RefArch";
292: // client configuration parameters
293: const config = {
294: headers: {},
295: parameters: {
296: clientId: CLIENT_ID,
297: organizationId: ORG_ID,
298: shortCode: SHORT_CODE,
299: siteId: SITE_ID,
300: },
301: };
302: /**
303: * Get the shopper or guest JWT/access token, along with a refresh token, using client credentials
304: *
305: * @returns guest user authorization token
306: */
307: async function getGuestUserAuthToken(): Promise<ShopperLoginTypes.TokenResponse> {
308: const base64data = Buffer.from(`${CLIENT_ID}:${CLIENT_SECRET}`).toString("base64");
309: const headers = { Authorization: `Basic ${base64data}` };
310: const loginClient = new ShopperLogin(config);
311: return await loginClient.getAccessToken({
312: headers,
313: body: { grant_type: "client_credentials" },
314: });
315: }
316: // Alternatively you may use the SLAS helper functions to generate JWT/access token
317: const guestTokenResponse = await slasHelpers.loginGuestUser({
318: slasClient: new ShopperLogin(config),
319: parameters: { redirectURI: 'http://localhost:3000/callback' }
320: })
321: .then((guestTokenResponse) => {
322: console.log("Guest Token Response: ", guestTokenResponse);
323: return guestTokenResponse;
324: })
325: .catch(error => console.log("Error fetching token for guest login: ", error));
326: // Get a JWT to use with Shopper API clients
327: getGuestUserAuthToken().then(async (token) => {
328: // Add the token to the client configuration
329: config.headers["authorization"] = `Bearer ${token.access_token}`;
330: const searchClient = new ShopperSearch(config);
331: // Search for dresses
332: const searchResults = await searchClient.productSearch({
333: parameters: { q: "dress", limit: 5 }
334: });
335: if (searchResults.total) {
336: const firstResult = searchResults.hits[0];
337: console.log(`${firstResult.productId} ${firstResult.productName}`);
338: } else {
339: console.log("No results for search");
340: }
341: return searchResults;
342: }).catch(async (e) => {
343: console.error(e);
344: console.error(await e.response.text());
345: });
346: SLAS helpers
347: The SDK includes helper functions to help developers easily onboard SLAS onto their applications to assist with authentication. A brief example is shown in the sample code above. The SLAS helpers offer both public and private client functions, the main difference being the private client functions require a client_secret. Code examples on how to use the different functions can be found the in the examples folder (examples 05 and 06). More information about SLAS and public/private client flows can be found here.
348: Error Handling
349: SDK methods return an appropriate object by default when the API call returns a successful response. The object is built from the body of the response. If the API response is not successful, an Error is thrown. The error message is set to the status code plus the status text. The Error object includes a custom 'response' attribute with the entire Response object for inspection.
350: try {
351: await productClient.getProduct({
352: parameters: {
353: id: "non-existant-id"
354: }
355: });
356: } catch (e) {
357: console.error(await e.response.text());
358: }
359: {
360: "title": "Product Not Found",
361: "type": "https://api.commercecloud.salesforce.com/documentation/error/v1/errors/product-not-found",
362: "detail": "No product with ID 'non-existant-id' for site 'RefArch' could be found.",
363: "productId": "non-existant-id",
364: "siteId": "RefArch"
365: }
366: Autocompletion
367: When using an IDE such as VSCode, the autocomplete feature lets you view the available method and class definitions, including parameters.
368: ​
369: To view the details of a method or a variable, hover over methods and variables.
370: ​
371: Autocomplete also shows the available properties of the data returned by SDK methods.
372: Fetch Options
373: Fetch options are able to be passed on to modify the behavior of the fetch call. There are two ways to pass on fetch options:
374: Through the client config
375: const config = {
376: parameters: {
377: clientId: CLIENT_ID,
378: organizationId: ORG_ID,
379: shortCode: SHORT_CODE,
380: siteId: SITE_ID,
381: },
382: fetchOptions: {
383: redirect: "error",
384: }
385: }
386: Through the SDK function call
387: const client = new ShopperLogin(config);
388: client.authorizeCustomer({
389: headers: { ... },
390: body: { ... },
391: fetchOptions: {
392: redirect: "manual"
393: }
394: });
395: If both the client config and the function call define the same fetch option with different values, the fetch option value for the function call will take priority. In the examples above, both pass in the redirect fetch option with different values, however, redirect: "manual" will take precedence because it was passed on the function call level.
396: Custom Query Parameters
397: With the introduction of hooks for Commerce APIs, customers can pass custom query parameters through the SDK to be used in their custom hook. Custom query parameters must begin with c_:
398: const searchResults = await searchClient.productSearch({
399: parameters: {
400: q: "dress",
401: limit: 5,
402: c_paramkey: '<param-value>'
403: }
404: });
405: Invalid query parameters that are not a part of the API and do not follow the c_ custom query parameter convention will be filtered from the request and a warning will be displayed.
406: Custom APIs
407: The SDK supports calling custom APIs with a helper function, customApiHelper.callCustomEndpoint().
408: Example usage:
409: import * as CommerceSdk from "commerce-sdk";
410: const { helpers } = CommerceSdk;
411: // client configuration parameters
412: const clientConfigExample = {
413: parameters: {
414: clientId: '<your-client-id>',
415: organizationId: '<your-org-id>',
416: shortCode: '<your-short-code>',
417: siteId: '<your-site-id>',
418: },
419: // If not provided, it'll use the default production URI:
420: // 'https://{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com/custom/{apiName}/{apiVersion}'
421: // path parameters should be wrapped in curly braces like the default production URI
422: baseUri: '<your-base-uri>'
423: };
424: const access_token = '<INSERT_ACCESS_TOKEN_HERE>'
425: // Required params: apiName, endpointPath, shortCode, organizaitonId
426: // Required path params can be passed into:
427: // options.customApiPathParameters or clientConfig.parameters
428: // customApiPathParameters will take priority for duplicate values
429: const customApiArgs = {
430: apiName: 'loyalty-info',
431: apiVersion: 'v1', // defaults to v1 if not provided
432: endpointPath: 'customers'
433: }
434: const getResponse = await helpers.callCustomEndpoint({
435: options: {
436: // http operation is defaulted to 'GET' if not provided
437: method: 'GET',
438: parameters: {
439: queryParameter: 'queryParameter1',
440: },
441: headers: {
442: // Content-Type is defaulted to application/json if not provided
443: 'Content-type': 'application/json',
444: authorization: `Bearer ${access_token}`
445: },
446: customApiPathParameters: customApiArgs,
447: },
448: clientConfig: clientConfigExample,
449: // Flag to retrieve raw response or data from helper function
450: rawResponse: false
451: })
452: const postResponse = await customApiHelper.callCustomEndpoint({
453: options: {
454: method: 'POST',
455: headers: {
456: authorization: `Bearer ${access_token}`
457: },
458: customApiPathParameters: {
459: apiVersion: 'v1',
460: endpointPath: 'greeting',
461: apiName: 'e2e-tests',
462: },
463: // When this flag is set to true, the request body will be automatically
464: // formatted in the expected format set by the 'Content-type' headers
465: // 'application/json' or 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'
466: enableTransformBody: true,
467: // object can be passed since we have enableTransformBody set to true
468: body: { data: 'data' }
469: // if enableTransformBody is not set to true,
470: // we have to ensure the request body is correctly formatted
471: // body: JSON.stringify({ data: 'data' })
472: },
473: clientConfig: clientConfigExample,
474: rawResponse: false
475: })
476: console.log('get response: ', getResponse)
477: console.log('post response: ', postResponse)
478: Encoding special characters
479: The SDK currently single encodes special characters for query parameters in UTF-8 format based on SCAPI guidelines. However, the SDK does NOT encode path parameters, and will require the developer to encode any path parameters with special characters.
480: Additionally, SCAPI has special characters that should be double encoded, specifically % and ,:
481: % should always be double encoded
482: , should be double encoded when used as part of an ID/parameter string, and single encoded when used to differentiate items in a list
483: There is a helper function called encodeSCAPISpecialCharacters that can be utilized to single encode the SCAPI special characters and no other special characters.
484: Here's an example where the getCategory/getCategories endpoints are called with a categoryID with special characters:
485: import * as CommerceSdk from "commerce-sdk";
486: const { helpers, Product } = CommerceSdk;
487: const clientConfig = {
488: parameters: {
489: clientId: "<your-client-id>",
490: organizationId: "<your-org-id>",
491: shortCode: "<your-short-code>",
492: siteId: "<your-site-id>",
493: }
494: };
495: const shopperProducts = new Product.ShopperProducts({
496: ...clientConfig,
497: headers: {authorization: `Bearer <insert_access_token>`}
498: });
499: const categoryId = "SpecialCharacter,%$^@&$;()!123Category";
500: // "SpecialCharacter%2C%25$^@&$;()!123Category"
501: const scapiSpecialEncodedId = helpers.encodeSCAPISpecialCharacters(categoryId);
502: // id is a path parameter for API call:
503: // <base-url>/product/shopper-products/v1/organizations/{organizationId}/categories/{id}
504: const categoryResult = await shopperProducts.getCategory({
505: parameters: {
506: // Path parameters are NOT encoded by the SDK, so we have to single encode special characters
507: // and the SCAPI special characters will end up double encoded
508: id: encodeURIComponent(scapiSpecialEncodedId),
509: }
510: });
511: console.log("categoryResult: ", categoryResult);
512: // `ids` are a query parameter and comma delimited to separate category IDs
513: const categoriesResult = await shopperProducts.getCategories({
514: parameters: {
515: // No need to use `encodeURIComponent` as query parameters are single encoded by the SDK
516: // So the SCAPI special characters will end up double encoded as well
517: // Commas that separate items in a list will end up single encoded
518: ids: `${scapiSpecialEncodedId},${scapiSpecialEncodedId}`,
519: }
520: });
521: console.log("categoriesResult: ", categoriesResult);
522: NOTE: In the next major version release, path parameters will be single encoded by default
523: Caching
524: The SDK currently supports two types of caches - In-memory and Redis. Both the implementations respect standard cache headers. To use another type of cache, write your own implementation of the CacheManager. See the default cache manager to design your implementation.
525: Cache storage adapter
526: The default cache storage is limited to 10,000 distinct entities before applying a simple least recently used policy for cache replacement. The limit can be changed by creating a quick-lru storage adapter.
527: import { CacheManagerKeyv } from '@commerce-apps/core';
528: import { QuickLRU } from 'quick-lru';
529: const cacheManagerKeyv = new CacheManagerKeyv({
530: keyvStore: new QuickLRU({ maxSize: 50000 }),
531: });
532: const config = {
533: cacheManager: cacheManagerKeyv,
534: parameters: {
535: clientId: '<your-client-id>',
536: organizationId: '<your-org-id>',
537: shortCode: '<your-short-code>',
538: siteId: '<your-site-id>'
539: },
540: };
541: See these directions to create a cache storage adapter.
542: In-memory cache
543: In-memory caching of responses is enabled by default. To disable caching for a client, set cacheManager to 'null'.
544: const config = {
545: cacheManager: null,
546: parameters: {
547: clientId: '<your-client-id>',
548: organizationId: '<your-org-id>',
549: shortCode: '<your-short-code>',
550: siteId: '<your-site-id>'
551: },
552: };
553: Redis cache
554: To use a Redis cache, instantiate a CacheManagerRedis object with a Redis URL and add it to your client config object.
555: import { CacheManagerRedis } from '@commerce-apps/core';
556: const cacheManager = new CacheManagerRedis({
557: connection: 'redis://localhost:6379',
558: });
559: const config = {
560: cacheManager: cacheManager,
561: parameters: {
562: clientId: '<your-client-id>',
563: organizationId: '<your-org-id>',
564: shortCode: '<your-short-code>',
565: siteId: '<your-site-id>'
566: },
567: };
568: Memory management
569: Redis can be configured to apply an eviction policy when the specified memory limit is reached. See this article to set up Redis as an LRU cache and to learn more about supported eviction policies.
570: Retry Policies
571: Use the node-retry package to facilitate request retries. The following retry type definition is taken from the node-retry package.
572: type RetrySettings = {
573: /**
574: * Whether to retry forever.
575: * @default false
576: */
577: forever?: boolean;
578: /**
579: * Whether to [unref](https://nodejs.org/api/timers.html#timers_unref) the setTimeout's.
580: * @default false
581: */
582: unref?: boolean;
583: /**
584: * The maximum time (in milliseconds) that the retried operation is allowed to run.
585: * @default Infinity
586: */
587: maxRetryTime?: number;
588: /**
589: * The maximum amount of times to retry the operation.
590: * @default 10
591: */
592: retries?: number;
593: /**
594: * The exponential factor to use.
595: * @default 2
596: */
597: factor?: number;
598: /**
599: * The number of milliseconds before starting the first retry.
600: * @default 1000
601: */
602: minTimeout?: number;
603: /**
604: * The maximum number of milliseconds between two retries.
605: * @default Infinity
606: */
607: maxTimeout?: number;
608: /**
609: * Randomizes the timeouts by multiplying a factor between 1-2.
610: * @default false
611: */
612: randomize?: boolean;
613: };
614: All options can be set per client or per request.
615: Example:
616: productClient = new Product({
617: retrySettings: {
618: // This means 3 total calls are made
619: retries: 2,
620: // Max wait between retries
621: maxTimeout: 200,
622: // Min wait between retries
623: minTimeout: 100
624: }
625: }
626: Logging
627: Default log level of the SDK is WARN (warning). SDK uses loglevel npm package. All the log levels supported by loglevel package are supported in SDK.
628: To change the loglevel, set the desired level on the SDK logger.
629: import { sdkLogger } from 'commerce-sdk';
630: sdkLogger.setLevel(sdkLogger.levels.INFO);
631: INFO level logging enables:
632: brief request and response logging
633: DEBUG level logging enables logging of:
634: fetch options
635: curl command of the request
636: response (response body is not included)
637: cache operations
638: Note: Debug level logging may expose sensitive data in the logs
639: Security
640: This library doesn't store or refresh authentication tokens. Storing and refreshing authentication tokens is the responsibility of the SDK consumer.
641: This library limits its runtime dependencies to reduce the total cost of ownership as much as possible. However, we recommend that you have security stakeholders review all third-party products (3PP) and their dependencies.
642: For more information about security considerations related to developing headless commerce applications, see
643: Security Considerations for Headless Commerce on the
644: Commerce Cloud Developer Center.
645: If you discover any potential security issues, please report them to security@salesforce.com as soon as possible.

212: commerce-sdk-isomorphic
213: This SDK provides a Browser & Node.js JavaScript client for calling B2C Commerce Shopper APIs.
214: For a Node.js only SDK that can also access Admin APIs checkout Commerce SDK.
215: Documentation
216: An auto-generated documentation site provides comprehensive reference for all available endpoints and types across API classes. Following the v4.0.0 release, the underlying SDK file structure has been reorganized, introducing additional layers of imports/exports that may affect navigation.
217: Navigating the Documentation
218: For API Classes:
219: Accessing API Classes: Click on the API class name (e.g., shopperProducts) on the right hand side
220: Viewing Endpoints: Scroll to the Classes section and click the corresponding API class link (e.g., ShopperProducts) to see available endpoints and their parameters
221: Type Definitions: Scroll to the Type aliases section for available types
222: Utility Classes: Utility classes and methods such as clientConfig and helpers maintain the same structure as previous versions.
223: NOTES:
224: Type Access: API class types are accessible through the <api_class>Types namespace (e.g., ShopperProductsTypes). Individual types can be accessed as ShopperProductsTypes.Product.
225: Type References: The References section under API classes in the generated documentation may show duplicate entries. This occurs because types are exported both at their original definition and under the API class namespace. Both references point to the same underlying type definition.
226: ⚠️ Planned API Changes ⚠️
227: Shopper Context
228: Starting July 31st 2024, all endpoints in the Shopper context API will require the siteId parameter for new customers. This field is marked as optional for backward compatibility and will be changed to mandatory tentatively by January 2025. You can read more about the planned change here in the notes section.
229: Shopper Login (SLAS)
230: SLAS will soon require new tenants to pass channel_id as an argument for retrieving guest access tokens. You can read more about the planned change here.
231: Please be aware that existing tenants are on a temporary allow list and will see no immediate disruption to service. We do ask that all users seek to adhere to the channel_id requirement before the end of August to enhance your security posture before the holiday peak season.
232: In practice, we recommend:
233: For customers using the SLAS helpers with a public client, it is recommended to upgrade to at least v1.8.0 of the commerce-sdk-isomorphic.
234: For customers using the SLAS helpers with a private client, it is recommended to upgrade to v3.0.0 of the commerce-sdk-isomorphic.
235: ⚠️ Planned SDK Changes ⚠️
236: Encoding path parameters
237: In the next major version release, the SDK will encode special characters (UTF-8 based on SCAPI guidelines) in path parameters by default. Please see the Encoding special characters section for more details.
238: Migration off node-fetch
239: node-fetch@2 is maintenance-only, and the upstream Node.js fix for the keep-alive regression (see Node.js version compatibility) works around but does not remove the underlying node-fetch heuristic. A future release will replace node-fetch on the server path with the Node.js built-in fetch (available in Node 18 and later, which the SDK's current ^20.x/^22.x requirement already satisfies). This will change how custom agent options work (built-in fetch is backed by undici and does not accept an http.Agent/https.Agent), and continue to honor a caller-supplied fetch via the fetch client-config option.
240: Getting Started
241: Requirements
242: Node ^20.x or ^22.x
243: The SDK requires B2C Commerce API (SCAPI) to be configured. For more info see Getting started with SCAPI.
244: Node.js version compatibility
245: A regression in Node.js 24.17.0 and 22.23.0 caused libraries built on node-fetch@2 to throw false ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE ("Premature close") errors when reusing keep-alive connections under load. The security fix in those releases added a listener to the socket 'data' event, which node-fetch@2 misreads as a truncated response (nodejs/node#63989). It is most likely to surface on gzip-compressed, chunked responses such as large SCAPI product or search payloads.
246: Note: commerce-sdk-isomorphic is affected on the server (Node.js) path, because it makes HTTP requests using node-fetch@2. Browser builds use the platform fetch and are not affected. (The companion Commerce SDK, whose HTTP layer is make-fetch-happen, is not affected.)
247: To resolve it, upgrade to a Node.js release that contains the upstream fix: on the 24.x line use 24.18.0 or later (avoid 24.17.0); on the 22.x line use 22.23.1 or later (avoid 22.23.0). Versions before the regression (24.16.0 and earlier, 22.22.x and earlier) do not have this bug, but they also predate the security fix it shipped alongside, so upgrade forward rather than downgrading.
248: If you cannot change your Node.js version, avoid enabling keep-alive on the agent you pass through fetchOptions (the bug only occurs when a pooled socket is reused). This removes connection pooling and adds a TLS handshake per request.
249: Newer "Current"-line releases (Node 26.x) that shipped the same security patch are affected as well. As of June 24, 2026 no fixed 26.x release had shipped; check the Node 26.x changelog for a release that contains the upstream fix. For production, prefer an LTS line (24.x or 22.x) on the fixed versions above.
250: References:
251: Regression: nodejs/node#63989 · Upstream fix: nodejs/node#64004
252: Fixed releases: v24.18.0, v22.23.1
253: Underlying node-fetch issue (open): node-fetch#1767
254: Installation
255: # This package uses yarn, if you don't have yarn:
256: # npm install -g yarn
257: yarn install commerce-sdk-isomorphic
258: Usage
259: import {helpers, ShopperLogin, ShopperSearch} from 'commerce-sdk-isomorphic';
260: const config = {
261: // SCAPI does not support CORS, so client side requests must use a reverse proxy.
262: proxy: 'https://localhost:3000',
263: parameters: {
264: clientId: '<your-client-id>',
265: organizationId: '<your-org-id>',
266: shortCode: '<your-short-code>',
267: siteId: '<your-site-id>',
268: },
269: };
270: const {access_token} = await helpers.loginGuestUser({
271: slasClient: new ShopperLogin(config),
272: parameters: {redirectURI: `${config.proxy}/callback`}
273: });
274: const shopperSearch = new ShopperSearch({
275: ...config,
276: headers: {authorization: `Bearer ${access_token}`},
277: });
278: const searchResult = await shopperSearch.productSearch({
279: parameters: {q: 'shirt'},
280: });
281: Fetch Options
282: You can configure how the SDK makes requests using the fetchOptions parameter. It is passed to node-fetch on the server and whatwg-fetch on browser.
283: const https = require("https");
284: const config = {
285: fetchOptions: {
286: // By default, requests made using the SDK do not include cookies.
287: credentials: "include",
288: timeout: 2000,
289: agent: new https.agent({ keepAlive: true }),
290: },
291: };
292: For more info, refer to the documentation site.
293: throwOnBadResponse
294: When true, the SDK throws an Error on responses whose status is not 2xx or 304. By default, the value of this flag is false for backwards compatibility. Below is an example for accessing the error object via e.response.json().
295: const config = {
296: throwOnBadResponse: true
297: // rest of the config object...
298: };
299: const shopperSearch = new ShopperSearch({
300: ...config
301: });
302: // in an async function
303: try {
304: const searchResult = await shopperSearch.productSearch({
305: parameters: { q: "shirt" },
306: });
307: } catch (e) {
308: const error = await e.response.json();
309: console.log(error);
310: // error is the JSON object - {error: ",,,"}
311: }
312: throwOnMaintenanceHeader
313: When true, the SDK automatically detects maintenance mode by checking the sfdc_maintenance response header. If the header value is 'system' or 'site', the SDK throws a MaintenanceError with status 503. This is useful for handling scheduled maintenance windows and displaying appropriate messaging to users. By default, this flag is false for backwards compatibility.
314: import {ShopperProducts, helpers} from 'commerce-sdk-isomorphic';
315: const {MaintenanceError} = helpers;
316: const config = {
317: throwOnMaintenanceHeader: true,
318: // rest of the config object...
319: };
320: const shopperProducts = new ShopperProducts(config);
321: // in an async function
322: try {
323: const product = await shopperProducts.getProduct({
324: parameters: {id: 'product-id'},
325: });
326: } catch (e) {
327: if (e instanceof MaintenanceError) {
328: console.log(`Service in maintenance: ${e.maintenanceType}`); // 'system' or 'site'
329: console.log(`Status: ${e.status}`); // 503
330: // Display maintenance page to user
331: } else {
332: // Handle other errors
333: console.error('API error:', e);
334: }
335: }
336: Note: The maintenance check occurs before other error handling and applies even when using rawResponse: true.
337: Additional Config Settings
338: headers: Headers to include with API requests.
339: Custom Query Parameters
340: You can pass custom query parameters through the SDK to be used in B2C Commerce API Hooks. Custom query parameters must begin with c_:
341: const searchResult = await shopperSearch.productSearch({
342: parameters: {
343: q: 'shirt',
344: c_paramkey: '<param-value>'
345: },
346: });
347: Invalid query parameters that are not a part of the API and do not follow the c_ custom query parameter convention are filtered from the request with a warning.
348: Custom APIs
349: The SDK supports calling B2C Commerce Custom APIs with a helper function, callCustomEndpoint:
350: import pkg from "commerce-sdk-isomorphic";
351: const { helpers } = pkg;
352: const clientConfig = {
353: parameters: {
354: clientId: "<your-client-id>",
355: organizationId: "<your-org-id>",
356: shortCode: "<your-short-code>",
357: siteId: "<your-site-id>",
358: },
359: // If not provided, it'll use the default production URI:
360: // 'https://{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com/custom/{apiName}/{apiVersion}'
361: // path parameters should be wrapped in curly braces like the default production URI
362: baseUri: "<your-base-uri>",
363: };
364: // Required params: apiName, endpointPath, shortCode, organizaitonId
365: // Required path params can be passed into:
366: // options.customApiPathParameters or clientConfig.parameters
367: const customApiPathParameters = {
368: apiName: "loyalty-info",
369: apiVersion: "v1", // defaults to v1 if not provided
370: endpointPath: "customers",
371: };
372: const accessToken = "<INSERT ACCESS TOKEN HERE>";
373: await helpers.callCustomEndpoint({
374: options: {
375: method: "GET",
376: parameters: {
377: queryParameter: "queryParameter1",
378: },
379: headers: {
380: // Content-Type is defaulted to application/json if not provided
381: "Content-Type": "application/json",
382: authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}`,
383: },
384: customApiPathParameters,
385: },
386: clientConfig,
387: });
388: await helpers.callCustomEndpoint({
389: options: {
390: method: "POST",
391: parameters: {
392: queryParameter: "queryParameter1",
393: },
394: headers: {
395: authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}`,
396: },
397: customApiPathParameters,
398: body: JSON.stringify({ data: "data" }),
399: },
400: clientConfig,
401: });
402: For more documentation about this helper function, please refer to the commerce-sdk-isomorphic docs.
403: Custom Fetch function
404: You can provide your own custom fetch function to intercept, log, or modify all SDK requests. This is useful for:
405: Request/Response Logging: Track all API calls for debugging and monitoring
406: Request Interception: Add custom headers, modify request URLs, or implement custom retry logic
407: Error Handling: Add custom error processing or transformation before responses reach your application
408: Performance Monitoring: Measure request/response times and track API performance metrics
409: Example with Logging:
410: // Custom fetch function with detailed logging
411: const customFetch = async (url, options) => {
412: console.log(`[SDK Request] ${options?.method || 'GET'} ${url}`);
413: console.log('[SDK Request Headers]', options?.headers);
414: if (options?.body) {
415: console.log('[SDK Request Body]', options.body);
416: }
417: const startTime = Date.now();
418: const response = await fetch(url, options);
419: const duration = Date.now() - startTime;
420: console.log(`[SDK Response] ${response.status} ${response.statusText} (${duration}ms)`);
421: console.log('[SDK Response Headers]', Object.fromEntries(response.headers.entries()));
422: return response;
423: };
424: const config = {
425: parameters: {
426: clientId: '<your-client-id>',
427: organizationId: '<your-org-id>',
428: shortCode: '<your-short-code>',
429: siteId: '<your-site-id>',
430: },
431: fetch: customFetch,
432: };
433: Encoding special characters
434: The SDK currently single encodes special characters for query parameters in UTF-8 format based on SCAPI guidelines. However, the SDK does NOT encode path parameters, and will require the developer to encode any path parameters with special characters.
435: Additionally, SCAPI has special characters that should be double encoded, specifically % and ,:
436: % should always be double encoded
437: , should be double encoded when used as part of an ID/parameter string, and single encoded when used to differentiate items in a list
438: There is a helper function called encodeSCAPISpecialCharacters that can be utilized to single encode the SCAPI special characters and no other special characters.
439: Here's an example where the getCategory/getCategories endpoints are called with a categoryID with special characters:
440: import pkg from "commerce-sdk-isomorphic";
441: const { helpers, ShopperProducts } = pkg;
442: const clientConfig = {
443: parameters: {
444: clientId: "<your-client-id>",
445: organizationId: "<your-org-id>",
446: shortCode: "<your-short-code>",
447: siteId: "<your-site-id>",
448: }
449: };
450: const shopperProducts = new ShopperProducts({
451: ...clientConfig,
452: headers: {authorization: `Bearer <insert_access_token>`}
453: });
454: const categoryId = "SpecialCharacter,%$^@&$;()!123Category";
455: // "SpecialCharacter%2C%25$^@&$;()!123Category"
456: const scapiSpecialEncodedId = helpers.encodeSCAPISpecialCharacters(categoryId);
457: // id is a path parameter for API call:
458: // <base-url>/product/shopper-products/v1/organizations/{organizationId}/categories/{id}
459: const categoryResult = await shopperProducts.getCategory({
460: parameters: {
461: // No need to use `encodeURIComponent` as query parameters are single encoded by the SDK
462: // So the SCAPI special characters will end up double encoded as well
463: id: scapiSpecialEncodedId,
464: }
465: });
466: console.log("categoryResult: ", categoryResult);
467: // `ids` are a query parameter and comma delimited to separate category IDs
468: const categoriesResult = await shopperProducts.getCategories({
469: parameters: {
470: // No need to use `encodeURIComponent` as query parameters are single encoded by the SDK
471: // So the SCAPI special characters will end up double encoded as well
472: // Commas that separate items in a list will end up single encoded
473: ids: `${scapiSpecialEncodedId},${scapiSpecialEncodedId}`,
474: }
475: });
476: console.log("categoriesResult: ", categoriesResult);
477: NOTE: In the next major version release, path parameters will be single encoded by default
478: Contributing
479: The SDK is generated from the SCAPI OAS specs that the ECOM monorepo publishes. To update them, see Updating APIs and the ECOM spec source contract.

26: Orders API overview
27: Current version: 1.0
28: For versioning details, read the Versioning guide.
29: Use the Orders API to access the order history for a Squarespace merchant site.
30: Orders can be one-time purchase orders and recurring orders generated by subscriptions.
31: The Orders API can also filter orders by Customer ID, import orders from third-party sales channels,
32: mark orders as fulfilled, and trigger shipment notifications.
33: Note: Although they appear in Squarespace as orders, the Orders API does not provide access to donations.
34: Instead, donation information can be accessed using the
35: Transactions API.
36: API resources
37: The Orders API returns order information in Order resource objects.
38: Resource fields are described under Response example for each Orders API endpoint.
39: Payment Plans
40: Squarespace supports Payment Plans on eligible products: an initial deposit collected at checkout, followed by a series of installments charged automatically on a seller-defined schedule. Shoppers select between paying in full and choosing a payment plan on the product details page (PDP), and only the deposit is collected at checkout. See the Add payment plans to service products Help Center article for the current eligibility rules and shopper experience.
41: A Payment Plan is represented as a single Order whose paymentState evolves as each installment is collected, rather than as separate orders per payment.
42: Payment state
43: Every Order exposes a paymentState field that reports the current payment state of the order.
44: ValueMeaning
45: NOT_CHARGEDThe order has been created but no payment has been attempted yet.
46: AUTHORIZEDA payment has been authorized but not captured.
47: PAIDThe order is fully paid. For a Payment Plan order, this means all installments have been collected.
48: PARTIALLY_PAIDA Payment Plan order with one or more installments still outstanding. An order enters this state as soon as the deposit is captured (before any installment has been collected) and remains in it while installments are still being collected.
49: PENDINGA payment is awaiting confirmation. The order will subsequently transition to PAID, PARTIALLY_PAID or FAILED.
50: FAILEDThe terminal state for an order whose payment was previously PENDING and ultimately did not succeed.
51: REFUND_PENDINGA refund has been initiated and is being processed. The order will subsequently transition to REFUNDED or REFUND_FAILED.
52: REFUNDEDThe order has had refund activity. This covers both full and partial refunds; a partial refund of any amount sets the order to REFUNDED. To determine the outstanding balance, compare the order's refundedTotal with grandTotal.
53: REFUND_FAILEDAn asynchronous refund attempt failed.
54: Filtering by payment state
55: The retrieve all orders endpoint accepts an optional paymentStates query parameter, a comma-separated list of the values above. If omitted, the endpoint defaults to NOT_CHARGED,AUTHORIZED,PAID,REFUNDED, which preserves the response set returned before Payment Plans existed and keeps existing integrations stable.
56: To include Payment Plan orders that are mid-collection, pass PARTIALLY_PAID explicitly:
57: Code
58: GET /1.0/commerce/orders?paymentStates=PAID,PARTIALLY_PAID
59: Working with Payment Plan orders
60: A few practical notes when integrating against Payment Plan orders:
61: Cancellations and refunds: sellers can cancel individual installments or an entire payment plan from the Orders panel. Canceling a plan stops future scheduled installments but does not automatically refund payments that have already been collected — those can be refunded individually. The Transactions API exposes per-payment refund detail.
62: Webhooks: to preserve backward compatibility with existing integrations, the order.create webhook for a Payment Plan order fires only when paymentState transitions to PAID (all installments collected), not when the order is initially placed. No webhook fires for the deposit or for intermediate installment captures. The order.update webhook continues to fire normally for FULFILLED, REFUNDED, CANCELED, MARKED_PENDING, and EMAIL_UPDATED events at any point in the order's lifecycle. For real-time visibility into newly placed Payment Plan orders, use the retrieve all orders endpoint with paymentStates=PARTIALLY_PAID.

172: Gumroad CLI
173: CLI for the Gumroad API. Designed for humans and AI agents alike.
174: Install
175: brew install antiwork/cli/gumroad
176: On Windows, download gumroad-cli_windows_amd64.zip or gumroad-cli_windows_arm64.zip, unzip it, and put gumroad.exe on your PATH. In PowerShell:
177: Invoke-WebRequest https://github.com/antiwork/gumroad-cli/releases/latest/download/gumroad-cli_windows_amd64.zip -OutFile gumroad-cli.zip
178: Expand-Archive .\gumroad-cli.zip -DestinationPath "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\gumroad"
179: $env:Path = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\gumroad;$env:Path"
180: [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\gumroad;" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User"), "User")
181: gumroad auth login
182: Use Windows Terminal or PowerShell. Quote paths that contain spaces (& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\gumroad\gumroad.exe"). If SmartScreen blocks gumroad.exe, choose More info → Run anyway. Homebrew and the curl installer do not apply to stock PowerShell.
183: Other installation methods
184: # Shell script (macOS, Linux, and Windows Git Bash / MSYS2)
185: curl -fsSL https://gumroad.com/install-cli.sh | bash
186: # Go
187: go install github.com/antiwork/gumroad-cli/cmd/gumroad@latest
188: # From source (default prefix)
189: make install
190: # From source (custom prefix)
191: make install PREFIX="$HOME/.local"
192: Quick start
193: # Authenticate with device approval
194: gumroad auth login
195: # Or use an environment variable for CI / agents
196: export GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN=your-token
197: # View your account
198: gumroad user
199: # View or set your account refund policy
200: gumroad refund-policy view
201: gumroad refund-policy set --period 30 --fine-print "Refund requests are reviewed within 2 business days."
202: # List products, then inspect one
203: gumroad products list
204: gumroad products view abc123
205: # Fetch all sales, filter with jq
206: gumroad sales list --all --json --jq '.sales[] | {email, formatted_total_price}'
207: # Show sales totals
208: gumroad sales summary --group-by month --from 2026-01-01 --to 2026-05-21
209: # Preview a refund without executing it
210: gumroad sales refund abc123 --amount 5.00 --dry-run
211: Authentication
212: gumroad auth login starts OAuth device authorization. It prints a Gumroad approval URL, waits while you approve in the browser, then stores the seller token locally. Approve promptly and run one login at a time; Gumroad rate limits login requests per network address, so never put the command in a retry loop.
213: gumroad auth login # Device authorization (default)
214: gumroad auth login --web # Local browser OAuth
215: gumroad auth login --with-token < token.txt
216: gumroad auth status # Check seller auth and stored admin auth
217: gumroad auth token # Print the active seller token
218: gumroad auth logout # Revoke/delete stored tokens
219: For CI and agents with an existing token, set GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN or pipe the token into gumroad auth login --with-token; GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN takes precedence over stored seller config and needs no interactive login. Use --web only when you specifically want the local browser PKCE flow.
220: Commands
221: Run gumroad --help and gumroad <command> --help for subcommands, usage details, and examples.
222: Admin commands use a separate internal token. Run gumroad auth login --web and check the admin box to store one locally, or use GUMROAD_ADMIN_TOKEN with --non-interactive in CI and agent runs. For local testing, set GUMROAD_ADMIN_API_BASE_URL.
223: Which token does a command use?
224: Command group
225: Token
226: Env var
227: user, products, sales, files, subscribers, payouts, licenses, offercodes, webhooks, …
228: Seller access token
229: GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN
230: gumroad admin …
231: Admin token (separate credential)
232: GUMROAD_ADMIN_TOKEN
233: The two are not interchangeable. If a seller command fails with not_authenticated while GUMROAD_ADMIN_TOKEN is set — either alone, or copied into GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN — you need a seller token: set GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN to a seller token or run gumroad auth login.
234: Output modes
235: Flag
236: Output
237: Use case
238: (default)
239: Colored, formatted output
240: Human reading
241: --json
242: JSON
243: Programmatic access
244: --jq <expr>
245: Filtered JSON
246: Extract specific fields
247: --plain
248: Tab-separated, control chars escaped
249: Piping to grep/awk
250: --quiet
251: Minimal
252: Scripts
253: Paginated commands (sales list, payouts list, subscribers list) accept --all to fetch every page. Use --page-delay 200ms to pace large fetches.
254: AI agents
255: gumroad is built to work with AI agents. The --json, --jq, --no-input, and --non-interactive flags make it easy to query Gumroad data programmatically. Agents can start fresh seller auth with gumroad auth login and hand the printed approval URL to a human, or use GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN for a no-persistence auth path when a token already exists.
256: For MCP clients, run gumroad mcp. See connection setup and safety notes.
257: An agent skill is included. Run gumroad skill to install or refresh it.
258: Development
259: make build # Compile to ./gumroad
260: make test # Run all tests
261: make test-cover # Tests with per-package coverage gates (85% cmd, 90% infra)
262: make test-smoke # Live read-only smoke test against real API
263: make lint # golangci-lint
264: make man # Generate man pages
265: make snapshot # Build release snapshot via goreleaser
266: Live smoke test:
267: GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN=your-token make test-smoke

156: Gumroad MCP Server
157: gumroad-mcp-60.mp4
158: Overview
159: A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server implementation for Gumroad, enabling MCP-compatible AI clients like Claude Desktop to interact with Gumroad API.
160: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) allows AI assistants to interact with external tools and services.
161: Quickstart
162: Start using Gumroad MCP Server with Claude Desktop in seconds:
163: npx gumroad-mcp@latest init
164: This command sets up the MCP server with your Gumroad credentials through an interactive prompt.
165: Usage
166: Once configured, try these commands in your MCP-compatible client:
167: How many sales did I make last month vs a year ago?
168: Generate an interactive chart with last year's sales
169: List my top-selling products on Gumroad from last year
170: Show month-over-month trend of my top-selling product last year
171: Disable "Product Name" product
172: Enable "Product Name" product
173: List all offer codes for "Product Name"
174: Create a new offer code "FAFO" with 99% off for "Product Name"
175: Delete offer code "abc123" from "Product Name"
176: Tools
177: Products
178: gumroad_get_products - Get all products
179: gumroad_get_product - Get a single product by ID
180: gumroad_disable_product - Disable a product
181: gumroad_enable_product - Enable a product
182: Sales
183: gumroad_get_sales - Get sales data
184: Offer Codes
185: gumroad_get_offer_codes - Get all offer codes for a product
186: gumroad_get_offer_code - Get a single offer code
187: gumroad_create_offer_code - Create a new offer code
188: gumroad_update_offer_code - Update an existing offer code
189: gumroad_delete_offer_code - Delete an offer code
190: User
191: gumroad_get_user - Get authenticated user data
192: Installation
193: Installing via Smithery
194: To install gumroad-mcp for Claude Desktop automatically via Smithery:
195: npx -y @smithery/cli install @rmarescu/gumroad-mcp --client claude
196: Prerequisites
197: Node.js 18 or later
198: A Gumroad account with API access
199: An MCP-compatible client (like Claude Desktop)
200: To verify you have Node installed, open the command line on your computer.
201: On macOS, open the Terminal from your Applications folder
202: On Windows, press Windows + R, type "cmd", and press Enter
203: Once in the command line, verify you have Node installed by entering in the following command:
204: node --version
205: Generate a Gumroad access token
206: Gumroad API requires authentication. To generate an access token, follow these steps:
207: Log in to your Gumroad account (or your own instance of Gumroad).
208: Go to Settings > Advanced page.
209: Create a new application by providing the following information:
210: Application icon (optional): A small thumbnail image to identify your application.
211: Application name: A name for your application.
212: Redirect URI: For personal use, you can enter http://127.0.0.1 (localhost) as this value is not meaningful in this context.
213: Click "Create application."
214: Use the "Generate access token" button to get your access token.
215: Keep your access token safe and confidential, like a password. You'll need to include it in your configuration as shown below.
216: Claude Desktop installation
217: If you use Claude Desktop, you can use the interactive setup:
218: npx gumroad-mcp@latest init
219: Manual installation
220: For other MCP-enabled applications, you will need to update the MCP configuration manually.
221: Example config
222: {
223: "mcpServers": {
224: "gumroad": {
225: "command": "npx",
226: "args": ["-y", "gumroad-mcp@latest"],
227: "env": {
228: "GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN": "<YOUR_TOKEN>"
229: }
230: }
231: }
232: }
233: If you're using a self-hosted Gumroad instance, you can configure the server to connect to your custom URL via GUMROAD_BASE_URL:
234: {
235: "mcpServers": {
236: "gumroad": {
237: "command": "npx",
238: "args": ["-y", "gumroad-mcp@latest"],
239: "env": {
240: "GUMROAD_ACCESS_TOKEN": "<YOUR_TOKEN>",
241: "GUMROAD_BASE_URL": "https://example.com"
242: }
243: }
244: }
245: }
246: Note
247: The server automatically appends the API version (/v2) to your base URL. For example, with GUMROAD_BASE_URL="https://example.com", API requests will be sent to https://example.com/v2.
248: Please refer to these instructions on how to add the MCP Server to Claude Desktop.
249: Contributing
250: Found a bug or want to suggest a feature? Please open an issue or submit a pull request on GitHub.
251: License
252: This MCP server is licensed under the MIT License. This means you are free to use, modify, and distribute the software, subject to the terms and conditions of the MIT License. For more details, please see the LICENSE file in the project repository.

1: # Selling Partner API Documentation
2: > Welcome to Selling Partner API Documentation. Learn how to get started and build applications with Amazon's REST-based SP-API. Subscribe to updates via [RSS feed](http://developer-docs.amazon.com/sp-api/changelog.rss).
3: ## Documentation: Get Started
4: - [Welcome to SP-API Documentation](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/welcome.md): Information about how to use the SP-API documentation site, and quick links for SP-API content.
5: - [What is the Selling Partner API?](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/what-is-the-selling-partner-api.md): This topic describes the REST-based Selling Partner API.
6: - [Selling Partner API Onboarding Overview](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/selling-partner-api-onboarding-overview.md): Determine which Selling Partner API onboarding path applies to you.
7: - [Onboarding as a Developer](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/onboarding-overview.md): Integrate your applications with Amazon's selling platform by using the Selling Partner API.
8: - [Step 1: Prepare for Registration](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/onboarding-step-1-prepare-for-registration.md): Gather the information and resources that you need to become an SP-API developer.
9: - [Step 2: Create a Solution Provider Portal Account](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/onboarding-step-2-create-an-spp-account.md): Create a Solution Provider Portal account to manage your SP-API applications.
10: - [Step 3: Create a Developer Profile](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/onboarding-step-3-create-a-developer-profile.md): Create a developer profile to manage your preferences and permissions.
11: - [Step 4: Register a Sandbox Application](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/onboarding-step-4-register-your-first-sandbox-application.md): Register a sandbox application in the Solution Provider Portal.
12: - [Step 5: Make Your First Call to the SP-API Sandbox](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/onboarding-step-5-make-your-first-call-to-the-sp-api-sandbox.md): Send test requests and receive responses in the SP-API sandbox environment.
13: - [Step 6: Set up the Authorization Workflow](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/onboarding-step-6-set-up-the-authorization-workflow.md): Configure how sellers authorize your application to call the SP-API on their behalf.

15: - [Step 8: Call the SP-API in Production](https://developer-docs.amazon/sp-api/docs/onboarding-step-8-call-the-sp-api-in-production.md): Connect to the SP-API by using manual HTTP requests or an SDK.

600: SP-API Registration Overview
601: Learn how to register as an SP-API developer.
602: You must register as a Selling Partner API (SP-API) developer before you can register your Selling Partner API application.
603: The procedure for registering as a developer varies slightly depending on the type of application that you plan to create:
604: Private seller applications: Applications for sellers that are available only to your organization, and are self-authorized. Note that in Seller Central, you must have a professional selling account to develop SP-API private seller applications. Individual accounts are not eligible. You can upgrade your account to a professional plan at any time.
605: Private vendor applications: Vendor applications that are available only to your organization, and are self-authorized.
606: Public seller and vendor applications: Applications that are publicly available and are authorized by sellers or by vendors using OAuth. In accordance with the Solution Provider Portal Agreement, public developers must list their app in the Amazon Selling Partner Appstore.
607: ❗
608: Important
609: Public and private applications are subject to authorization limits and restrictions. For more information, refer to Authorization Limits.
610: You must be a primary account user to complete registration.
611: Registration resources
612: Before you register, review the following information:
613: Policy requirements: Review the Acceptable Use Policy (AUP), Data Protection Policy (DPP), and Solution Provider Portal Agreement at Policies and Agreements.
614: Security implementation:
615: Ensure that the tech team responsible for data security answers the security control questions of the developer profile application.
616: Review the Selling Partner API technical papers for detailed guidance on vulnerability management, network protection, and data encryption.
617: To understand key security controls for SP-API integration and how these controls relate to DPP provisions, see Key Security Control Guidance.
618: Website requirements: If you are registering as a public developer or service provider, ensure that your website meets the Website Guidelines for Public Developers and Service Providers.
619: Role selection: To understand which roles to request, review Selling Partner API Roles.
620: Application guidelines: Keep your developer profile application under the 500-word limit and write original content. Do not copy information from the AUP, DPP, or other Amazon policies.
621: Status tracking: For information about your registration status, refer to Developer Registration Request Status.
622: Profile updates: To learn how to update your developer profile, refer to Update Your Developer Profile in Solution Provider Portal.

600: Authorize Applications
601: Learn how to authorize SP-API applications.
602: Authorization is the process by which a selling partner grants your application permission to call the Selling Partner API (SP-API) on the selling partner's behalf. For example, when a selling partner authorizes your order management application, they give your application permission to retrieve their order data through the SP-API.
603: After the authorization process is complete, your application can obtain the credentials that the SP-API requires for each API call.
604: This topic provides an overview of the available authorization methods and refers you to the relevant documentation based on the method that you choose.
605: Authorization methods
606: Your authorization method choices depend on whether your application is public or private. The following section summarizes the authorization methods. For details, refer to the specified documentation.
607: Public applications
608: Public applications are available to multiple selling partners through the selling partner's website or through the Selling Partner Appstore. The following information summarizes the available authorization methods for public applications:
609: Authorization method: OAuth 2.0 through Login with Amazon (LWA).
610: Who authorizes the application: The selling partner.
611: Initial authorization flow: The selling partner starts either from your website or from the Selling Partner Appstore. Through browser redirects, the selling partner interacts with both Amazon and your website to complete the authorization process.
612: Reauthorization: Reauthorization is required annually or if you want existing users (sellers or vendors) to authorize new roles for your application. To reauthorize your application, the selling partner starts at the Manage Your Apps page in Seller Central.
613: Developer implementation needed? Yes. You must implement an authorization and a reauthorization flow. The implementation involves setting up an OAuth login URI, an OAuth redirect URI, and so on.
614: Documentation:
615: Authorize Public Applications
616: Website Authorization Workflow
617: Selling Partner Appstore Authorization Workflow
618: Reauthorize Applications
619: Authorization Limits
620: Private applications
621: Private applications are for exclusive use by a single organization. The following information summarizes the available authorization methods for private applications:
622: Authorization method: Self-authorization.
623: Who authorizes the application: You.
624: Initial authorization flow: You perform a self-authorization process through Seller Central, Vendor Central, or the Solution Provider Portal.
625: Reauthorization: Reauthorization is required when you add new roles. You perform the self-authorization process through Seller Central, Vendor Central, or the Solution Provider Portal.
626: Developer implementation needed? No. You can perform authorization through one of the tools mentioned previously.
627: Documentation:
628: Authorize Private Applications
629: Revoke Self-Authorizations
630: Authorization Limits
631: 📘
632: Note
633: If you encounter issues while authorizing a Selling Partner API (SP-API) application, refer to Authorization error codes for troubleshooting steps and common error explanations.
634: Special cases
635: The following documentation applies to special cases:
636: Grantless operations: You can call some operations without explicit authorization from a selling partner. These operations are called grantless operations. For details, refer to Grantless Operations.
637: Vendor groups: For vendor applications, authorization applies to the group of vendor codes that are associated with the sign-in credentials for your Vendor Central account. For details about how to handle this case, refer to Authorize your Application to Access Vendor Groups.
638: Restricted data: Operations that access restricted data (such as Personally Identifiable Information) require authorization through a Restricted Data Token (RDT). For details, refer to Authorization with the Restricted Data Token.

600: Connect to the SP-API
601: How to connect to the SP-API.
602: These instructions show you the steps to connect to the Selling Partner API (SP-API). For links to additional examples, refer to SP-API SDKs.
603: Prerequisites
604: Before your application can connect to SP-API, you must:
605: Register the application. For details, refer to Registering your application.
606: Get the application authorized by a selling partner or, if you're a private developer, authorize it yourself. For details, refer to Authorizing Selling Partner API applications.
607: Step 1. Request a Login with Amazon access token
608: A Login with Amazon (LWA) access token authorizes your application to take certain actions on behalf of a selling partner. An LWA access token expires one hour after it is issued.
609: 📘
610: Note
611: An LWA access token must be included in calls to all operations except restricted operations, which return Personally Identifiable Information (PII). When calling restricted operations, instead of including an LWA access token, you include a Restricted Data Token (RDT). For information about getting RDTs and calling restricted operations, refer to the Tokens API Use Case Guide.
612: To request an LWA access token, make a secure HTTP POST to the LWA authentication server (https://api.amazon.com/auth/o2/token) with the following parameters:
613: NameDescriptionRequired
614: grant_typeThe type of access grant requested. Values:
615: - refresh_token. Use this for calling operations that require authorization from a selling partner. All operations that are not grantless operations require authorization from a selling partner. When specifying this value, include the refresh_token parameter.
616: - client_credentials. Use this for calling grantless operations. When specifying this value, include the scope parameter.Yes
617: refresh_tokenThe LWA refresh token. Get this value when the selling partner authorizes your application. For more information, refer to Authorizing Selling Partner API applications.No. Include refresh_token for calling operations that require authorization from a selling partner. If you include refresh_token, do not include scope.
618: scopeThe scope of the LWA authorization grant. Values:
619: Notifications API: sellingpartnerapi::notifications
620: Application Management API: sellingpartnerapi::client_credential:rotation
621: Tracking API: sellingpartnerapi::shipments:track
622: No. Include scope for calling a grantless operation. If you include scope, do not include refresh_token.
623: client_idGet this value when you register your application. Refer to Viewing your developer information.Yes
624: client_secretGet this value when you register your application. Refer to Viewing your developer information.Yes
625: Example for calling an operation that requires selling partner authorization:
626: HTTP
627: POST /auth/o2/token HTTP/l.l
628: Host: api.amazon.com
629: Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded;charset=UTF-8
630: grant_type=refresh_token
631: &refresh_token=Aztr|...
632: &client_id=foodev
633: &client_secret=Y76SDl2F
634: Example for calling a grantless operation:
635: HTTP
636: POST /auth/o2/token HTTP/l.l
637: Host: api.amazon.com
638: Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded;charset=UTF-8
639: grant_type=client_credentials
640: &scope=sellingpartnerapi::notifications
